Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Soldering Quality PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Soldering Quality by: Mila Nov 04,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb Layout pcb soldering pcb assembly pcb design guidelines PCB design plays an important role in soldering quality and overall assembly reliability. From component placement and pad design to fiducial marks and copper connections, even small layout details can affect solder paste printing, component placement, and reflow soldering. In this article, we'll explore key PCB layout guidelines to help reduce common soldering defects and improve SMT assembly efficiency. Factors Affecting PCB Soldering Quality Producing a high-quality PCB assembly involves multiple stages, from PCB design to component soldering. It requires coordination among PCB designers, process engineers, and production personnel. Several factors can affect PCB soldering quality, including PCB design files, board quality, component quality, oxidation on component leads, solder paste quality, solder paste printing accuracy, pick-and-place programming and placement accuracy, and the reflow oven temperature profile. Among these factors, PCB layout is one of the important elements that directly influence downstream assembly processes. PCB designers may have limited hands-on soldering and manufacturing experience, while production operators at assembly facilities are generally more focused on manufacturing tasks than on analyzing PCB design decisions. If manufacturing and soldering requirements are not considered during the design stage, unnecessary production difficulties may arise. Therefore, PCB designers should consider assembly processes and manufacturing requirements from the beginning to minimize potential problems during production. PCB Design Considerations for Better Soldering The following guidelines cover practical PCB layout considerations that can help reduce soldering defects and improve SMT assembly and repair efficiency. 1. Tooling Holes For PCBs that require SMT assembly, tooling holes can be added according to the requirements of the production equipment. They help secure and position the board during solder paste printing and subsequent manufacturing processes. Tooling holes are generally placed near the board corners or on the tooling edges. When multiple holes are used, their relative positions and machining accuracy should be carefully controlled to avoid positioning errors during production. The number, diameter, and location of tooling holes should be determined based on the PCB dimensions, panelization method, and equipment requirements. Four tooling holes at the corners are not mandatory for every PCB. 2. Fiducial Marks Fiducial marks should be provided on the PCB when required by the SMT equipment. They allow the pick-and-place machine to recognize the board's position and orientation through its vision system, improving component placement accuracy. Fiducial marks are commonly placed diagonally across the PCB and typically use circular exposed copper patterns. Sufficient clearance should be maintained around each mark to prevent nearby copper, pads, or silkscreen graphics from interfering with visual recognition. For double-sided SMT assembly, fiducial marks may be required on both sides, depending on the equipment and assembly process. For panelized PCBs, additional fiducial marks can also be placed on the tooling edges or panel to help the machine identify the entire panel. 3. Fiducial Mark Design Requirements When designing fiducial marks, consider the following points: a. Fiducial marks generally use solid circular exposed copper patterns. Their shape and dimensions should meet the requirements of the pick-and-place machine. b. A typical fiducial mark diameter is approximately 1.0 mm, although the exact size should follow the equipment manufacturer's specifications. c. Maintain a sufficient clearance around each fiducial mark. Avoid placing copper features, pads, silkscreen, or other patterns within this area. A clearance of approximately 1.0 mm around the mark is commonly used, subject to equipment requirements. d. The fiducial mark should provide sufficient contrast against the surrounding PCB surface to ensure reliable visual recognition. e. Keep the fiducial surface clean and flat. Oxidation, contamination, or excessive reflection may affect recognition accuracy. Exposed copper is commonly used, with the surface finish selected according to the PCB manufacturing process. Note that simple silkscreen outlines should not be used as substitutes for fiducial marks. Pick-and-place machines need to recognize a physical feature with a clearly defined boundary and optical characteristics. 4. Maintain Sufficient Clearance from PCB Edges PCB layouts should account for the conveying and clamping requirements of SMT equipment. For boards transported along conveyor rails, sufficient component-free space should be maintained near the board edges to prevent components from interfering with the rails or fixtures. Depending on the equipment, a clearance of approximately 3–5 mm from the board edge may be used as a reference. Avoid placing SMD components, protruding pads, or other features that may interfere with board handling in this area. For double-sided SMT assembly, also consider the risk of component movement or falling during the second reflow process, as well as potential interference between components and conveyor rails. If the PCB is too small to provide sufficient edge clearance, consider adding tooling edges to provide space for board transportation, positioning, and clamping. 5. Avoid Placing Vias Directly in Solder Pads Without Proper Treatment If an untreated via is placed directly within a conventional SMD pad, molten solder may flow into the via during reflow soldering. This can result in insufficient solder at the joint and, in severe cases, lead to weak or unreliable connections. Therefore, vias should generally be avoided directly within ordinary SMD pads. However, Via-in-Pad structures may be necessary for high-density layouts or specific component packages. In such cases, processes such as resin filling and copper capping can be used to prevent solder loss. 6. Polarity Markings for Diodes and Tantalum Capacitors Polarized components, such as diodes and tantalum capacitors, should have clearly defined polarity markings on the PCB to prevent incorrect placement during assembly or manual soldering. Polarity indicators must match the pin definitions in the component datasheet. Standard industry symbols should be used whenever possible. Even when PCB space is limited, ensure that polarity markings remain visible and are not covered by component bodies or other silkscreen graphics. 7. Silkscreen and Component Identification PCB silkscreen should be clear and concise. Avoid excessive component models, specifications, and other text that may make the board difficult to read, especially in high-density layouts. Component reference designators, such as R1, C1, and U1, should be retained whenever possible. They help production personnel identify component locations and make inspection and repair easier. Do not use component descriptions or part numbers without reference designators. This may increase the difficulty of pick-and-place programming and component identification during production. In addition, silkscreen text should not be too small. Place characters away from vias, pads, and other features that may interfere with readability. 8. IC Pad Length For IC packages with exposed leads, such as SOP, PLCC, and QFP, pad length should be determined based on the component lead dimensions and recommended footprint design. Appropriate pad dimensions help ensure proper solder paste printing, solder wetting, and reliable joint formation. They can also provide sufficient access for manual soldering and rework. However, using a fixed ratio, such as 1.5 times the IC lead length, is not recommended as a universal rule. Different package types have different lead structures and dimensions. Always refer to the recommended land pattern in the component datasheet or relevant IPC footprint design guidelines. 9. IC Pad Width For IC packages such as SOP, PLCC, and QFP, pad width and the spacing between adjacent pads directly affect soldering quality. Follow the recommended footprint dimensions in the component datasheet when determining pad width and spacing. Pads that are too wide or have insufficient spacing between them may increase the risk of solder bridging during assembly. For fine-pitch IC packages in particular, careful attention should be paid to pad dimensions, solder paste printing accuracy, and solder mask design. 10. Avoid Arbitrary Component Rotation During PCB layout, pay attention to component orientation and rotation angles. Keeping components of the same type oriented consistently can simplify pick-and-place programming, inspection, and maintenance. It is worth noting that modern pick-and-place machines generally support arbitrary component rotation angles and are not limited to 90°, 180°, or 270° increments. However, component rotation must be consistent with the footprint definition, coordinate files, and placement program. Otherwise, component leads may become misaligned with PCB pads, affecting placement and soldering quality. Pay particular attention to polarity when positioning diodes, electrolytic capacitors, and other polarized components. 11. Connecting Adjacent IC Pins When adjacent IC pins need to be electrically connected, the PCB layout should be designed carefully to avoid soldering problems and make inspection easier. Avoid simply merging multiple pad areas into one large copper region. Instead, use appropriate routing connections and solder mask openings according to the electrical requirements. Ensure that the soldering areas of individual pins remain clearly defined. Sufficient clearance must be maintained between pads that should not be electrically connected to prevent solder bridging. 12. Exposed Thermal Pads Under IC Packages Some IC packages, such as QFN and DFN, have an exposed thermal pad on the underside of the component. This pad is mainly used for heat dissipation and electrical grounding. When designing these packages, follow the recommended thermal pad dimensions in the component datasheet and consider the solder paste stencil design. If the thermal pad is too large and the entire area is covered with solder paste, excessive solder paste may cause problems such as solder voiding, component floating, or solder overflow during reflow. To reduce these risks, the solder paste opening can be divided into multiple smaller sections to control the amount of solder paste deposited. However, the thermal pad should not be arbitrarily reduced simply to prevent short circuits. Thermal performance, electrical connections, and soldering requirements must all be considered. 13. Avoid Placing Two Tall Components Too Close Together Component height and spacing should be considered during PCB layout. If two tall components are placed too close together, the pick-and-place machine may encounter interference when positioning the second component. The first component may obstruct the placement head or nozzle, affecting the placement process. Overcrowded layouts can also make inspection, soldering, and rework more difficult. Therefore, consider component height, package dimensions, nozzle clearance, and maintenance requirements when arranging taller components. Provide sufficient spacing to avoid mechanical interference. 14. BGA Design Considerations BGA components have solder balls underneath the package. Since these solder joints cannot be directly inspected from the outside after assembly, BGA packages require careful attention to PCB pad design, solder paste printing, and reflow soldering. When designing BGA footprints, strictly follow the component datasheet recommendations for pad dimensions, ball pitch, and PCB layout requirements. It is also important to consider inspection and rework requirements in advance. For example, additional positioning features may be needed on the PCB to accommodate BGA rework equipment and fixtures. If auxiliary tooling holes are required, their diameter, location, and spacing should match the actual rework equipment or alignment fixture. A single hole size should not be applied to every BGA design. 15. PCB Solder Mask Color Although solder mask color does not directly determine soldering quality, it may affect the visual recognition performance of SMT equipment. Different solder mask colors have different optical and reflective characteristics, which may influence how the machine's vision system recognizes fiducial marks and component positions. For example, certain dark solder mask colors may provide insufficient contrast under specific lighting conditions. Therefore, when selecting a PCB color, consider not only appearance but also compatibility with the production equipment's vision system. For unusual solder mask colors, confirm compatibility with the PCB manufacturer and SMT assembly provider in advance. 16. Small Components Under Large Components During PCB layout, avoid placing small components underneath large components when doing so may obstruct soldering, inspection, or rework. For example, if resistors or capacitors are placed underneath a seven-segment display or a large connector, technicians may need to remove the larger component before repairing the smaller one if a soldering defect occurs. This increases repair complexity and may damage the larger component or nearby pads during removal. Therefore, when circuit functionality and routing requirements allow, consider placing some small components on the opposite side of the PCB or repositioning them to provide better access for inspection and repair. 17. How Copper Pour Connections Affect Soldering When a PCB pad is directly connected to a large copper pour, heat may dissipate more rapidly during soldering. This can slow down pad heating and affect solder melting and wetting. This is particularly relevant for pads connected to large copper planes or internal power and ground layers. For example, in Figure A, the component pad is directly connected to a large copper area. In Figure B, although the connector pad is not directly connected to the copper pour, the large copper planes in the inner layers may still increase the overall thermal mass and affect soldering. If the reflow temperature is increased to compensate for excessive heat dissipation, temperature-sensitive connectors or plastic components may become deformed. Therefore, for pads that do not require direct high-current connections or special thermal performance, consider using thermal relief connections. These connections use narrow copper spokes to reduce heat dissipation and improve solderability. For high-current pads and thermal pads, however, current-carrying capacity, heat dissipation, and soldering requirements must be considered together. Thermal relief should not be applied indiscriminately. 18. PCB Panelization and Tooling Edge Design For small or irregularly shaped PCBs, panelization can improve SMT production efficiency by allowing multiple boards to be processed together. Several factors should be considered when designing PCB panels: Tooling Edge: Add tooling edges according to the conveying and clamping requirements of SMT equipment. This provides sufficient space for automated assembly. Fiducial Marks: Place fiducial marks on individual boards and the panel when required by the equipment to ensure accurate positioning. Tooling Holes: Add tooling holes as needed to keep the panel stable during manufacturing and assembly. Breakaway Methods: Select an appropriate separation method, such as V-scoring or mouse bites, based on the PCB structure and depanelization requirements. Component Clearance: Maintain sufficient clearance between components and separation areas to prevent mechanical stress from damaging components or solder joints during depanelization. A well-designed PCB panel can improve SMT production efficiency while reducing positioning errors and mechanical damage during assembly. Conclusion PCB layout should consider not only circuit functionality and electrical performance but also downstream manufacturing, soldering, inspection, and repair requirements. Proper fiducial mark placement, pad design, component arrangement, and panelization can help reduce potential problems during solder paste printing, SMT placement, and reflow soldering. PCB designers should therefore take actual manufacturing processes into account from the early design stage. A well-designed PCB should not only meet electrical requirements but also be easy to manufacture and assemble. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. If the thermal pad is too large and the entire area is covered with solder paste, excessive solder paste may cause problems such as solder voiding, component floating, or solder overflow during reflow. To reduce these risks, the solder paste opening can be divided into multiple smaller sections to control the amount of solder paste deposited. However, the thermal pad should not be arbitrarily reduced simply to prevent short circuits. Thermal performance, electrical connections, and soldering requirements must all be considered. 13. Avoid Placing Two Tall Components Too Close Together Component height and spacing should be considered during PCB layout. If two tall components are placed too close together, the pick-and-place machine may encounter interference when positioning the second component. The first component may obstruct the placement head or nozzle, affecting the placement process. Overcrowded layouts can also make inspection, soldering, and rework more difficult. Therefore, consider component height, package dimensions, nozzle clearance, and maintenance requirements when arranging taller components. Provide sufficient spacing to avoid mechanical interference. 14. BGA Design Considerations BGA components have solder balls underneath the package. Since these solder joints cannot be directly inspected from the outside after assembly, BGA packages require careful attention to PCB pad design, solder paste printing, and reflow soldering. When designing BGA footprints, strictly follow the component datasheet recommendations for pad dimensions, ball pitch, and PCB layout requirements. It is also important to consider inspection and rework requirements in advance. For example, additional positioning features may be needed on the PCB to accommodate BGA rework equipment and fixtures. If auxiliary tooling holes are required, their diameter, location, and spacing should match the actual rework equipment or alignment fixture. A single hole size should not be applied to every BGA design. 15. PCB Solder Mask Color Although solder mask color does not directly determine soldering quality, it may affect the visual recognition performance of SMT equipment. Different solder mask colors have different optical and reflective characteristics, which may influence how the machine's vision system recognizes fiducial marks and component positions. For example, certain dark solder mask colors may provide insufficient contrast under specific lighting conditions. Therefore, when selecting a PCB color, consider not only appearance but also compatibility with the production equipment's vision system. For unusual solder mask colors, confirm compatibility with the PCB manufacturer and SMT assembly provider in advance. 16. Small Components Under Large Components During PCB layout, avoid placing small components underneath large components when doing so may obstruct soldering, inspection, or rework. For example, if resistors or capacitors are placed underneath a seven-segment display or a large connector, technicians may need to remove the larger component before repairing the smaller one if a soldering defect occurs. This increases repair complexity and may damage the larger component or nearby pads during removal. Therefore, when circuit functionality and routing requirements allow, consider placing some small components on the opposite side of the PCB or repositioning them to provide better access for inspection and repair. 17. How Copper Pour Connections Affect Soldering When a PCB pad is directly connected to a large copper pour, heat may dissipate more rapidly during soldering. This can slow down pad heating and affect solder melting and wetting. This is particularly relevant for pads connected to large copper planes or internal power and ground layers. For example, in Figure A, the component pad is directly connected to a large copper area. In Figure B, although the connector pad is not directly connected to the copper pour, the large copper planes in the inner layers may still increase the overall thermal mass and affect soldering. If the reflow temperature is increased to compensate for excessive heat dissipation, temperature-sensitive connectors or plastic components may become deformed. Therefore, for pads that do not require direct high-current connections or special thermal performance, consider using thermal relief connections. These connections use narrow copper spokes to reduce heat dissipation and improve solderability. For high-current pads and thermal pads, however, current-carrying capacity, heat dissipation, and soldering requirements must be considered together. Thermal relief should not be applied indiscriminately. 18. PCB Panelization and Tooling Edge Design For small or irregularly shaped PCBs, panelization can improve SMT production efficiency by allowing multiple boards to be processed together. Several factors should be considered when designing PCB panels: Tooling Edge: Add tooling edges according to the conveying and clamping requirements of SMT equipment. This provides sufficient space for automated assembly. Fiducial Marks: Place fiducial marks on individual boards and the panel when required by the equipment to ensure accurate positioning. Tooling Holes: Add tooling holes as needed to keep the panel stable during manufacturing and assembly. Breakaway Methods: Select an appropriate separation method, such as V-scoring or mouse bites, based on the PCB structure and depanelization requirements. Component Clearance: Maintain sufficient clearance between components and separation areas to prevent mechanical stress from damaging components or solder joints during depanelization. A well-designed PCB panel can improve SMT production efficiency while reducing positioning errors and mechanical damage during assembly. Conclusion PCB layout should consider not only circuit functionality and electrical performance but also downstream manufacturing, soldering, inspection, and repair requirements. Proper fiducial mark placement, pad design, component arrangement, and panelization can help reduce potential problems during solder paste printing, SMT placement, and reflow soldering. PCB designers should therefore take actual manufacturing processes into account from the early design stage. A well-designed PCB should not only meet electrical requirements but also be easy to manufacture and assemble. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Guidelines for Special Component Placement PCB Layout Guidelines for Special Component Placement by: Mila Oct 26,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout is not an arbitrary process. It must follow certain design rules to ensure electrical performance, thermal management, and assembly quality. In addition to general layout requirements, some components have specific placement constraints that must be considered during PCB component placement. 1. Placement Requirements for Press-Fit Components For right-angle male and female press-fit components, no components taller than 3 mm should be placed within 3 mm of the component, and no soldered components should be placed within 1.5 mm. On the opposite side of the PCB, no components should be placed within 2.5 mm of the center of the press-fit pin holes. For straight male and female press-fit components, no components should be placed within 1 mm of the component. If a protective sleeve is required on the opposite side of the PCB, no components should be placed within 1 mm of the sleeve edge. If no sleeve is installed, no components should be placed within 2.5 mm of the press-fit holes. For hot-plug sockets used with grounding connectors in European-style connectors, components should not be placed within 6.5 mm of the front end of long pins or within 2.0 mm of the front end of short pins. For long pins on 2 mm FB single-pin power connectors, no components should be placed within 8 mm in front of the corresponding board-mounted socket. （Press-Fit Connector Placement and Clearance Requirements） 2. Placement Requirements for Temperature-Sensitive Components During PCB component placement, temperature-sensitive components should be kept away from high-heat components whenever possible. For example, electrolytic capacitors should be protected from prolonged exposure to excessive temperatures, while crystal oscillators require attention to temperature variations that may affect frequency stability. Components used for temperature sensing should be placed according to the target being measured and the actual heat-transfer path. They should be positioned to accurately reflect the target temperature while minimizing the influence of other heat-generating components, which could otherwise cause measurement errors or false triggering. Heat-generating components that can withstand high temperatures should be placed in locations that support effective heat dissipation, taking the actual airflow path into account. Components with limited heat resistance should be kept away from high-temperature areas. Where possible, avoid placing them directly in the airflow path downstream of other heat-generating components or where they may affect temperature-sensitive components. （PCB Layout for Thermal-Sensitive Components） 3. Placement Requirements for Polarized Components Through-hole devices (THD) with polarity or directional requirements should be oriented consistently and arranged neatly to facilitate insertion, soldering, and visual inspection. Surface-mount components (SMC) with polarity should preferably have a consistent orientation, provided that electrical connections and routing requirements are met. Components of the same type should be arranged neatly to simplify assembly and inspection. Common polarized components include electrolytic capacitors, tantalum capacitors, and diodes. During PCB layout, always verify component polarity markings against the schematic and PCB footprint to prevent circuit malfunctions caused by incorrect orientation. （Polarized Component Orientation in PCB Layout） 4. Placement Requirements for Through-Hole Reflow Components For PCBs with a dimension greater than 300 mm along the non-conveying edge, the placement of heavier components should be planned carefully, taking into account board thickness, support conditions, and component weight. Where appropriate, avoid placing heavy components in the center of the board to reduce the risk of PCB deformation and interference with component insertion or previously placed components. To facilitate component insertion, components may be placed closer to the insertion operation side, depending on the actual assembly process and equipment requirements. For long components, such as memory module sockets, the component's longitudinal axis should preferably be parallel to the PCB conveying direction, subject to the requirements of the production equipment and assembly process. The distance between the pad edges of through-hole reflow components and nearby QFPs, SOPs, connectors with a pitch of 0.65 mm or less, and all BGAs should be greater than 20 mm. The distance from other SMT components should be greater than 2 mm. These clearances should be verified against the actual soldering process and assembly manufacturer's requirements. The distance between the bodies of through-hole reflow components should be greater than 10 mm, subject to component dimensions and assembly process requirements. The distance between the pad edges of through-hole reflow components and the PCB conveying edge should be at least 10 mm. The distance from a non-conveying edge should be at least 5 mm. The design should also account for clamping areas, panelization, and production equipment constraints. Conclusion Proper PCB layout affects not only electrical performance but also thermal management, assembly efficiency, and product reliability. When developing PCB component placement guidelines, designers should consider component characteristics, electrical requirements, mechanical clearances, and manufacturing processes. Reviewing these factors against component datasheets and assembly requirements can help prevent placement conflicts, reduce manufacturing issues, and improve overall PCB design quality. Verify Now Blog > PCB Routing Guidelines for Ground, Power, and Signal Traces PCB Routing Guidelines for Ground, Power, and Signal Traces by: Mila Oct 22,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB routing PCB routing guidelines PCB trace routing PCB ground plane PCB signal integrity Poor PCB routing can lead to signal integrity issues, EMC failures, and power instability, even when component selection and schematic design are correct. These problems often stem from discontinuous return paths, improper trace routing, or insufficient consideration of electrical constraints. This article covers key PCB routing guidelines for ground planes, critical signals, and power traces, along with a practical routing workflow and common mistakes to help engineers improve design reliability and manufacturability. Understanding PCB Routing Priorities PCB routing should not follow a rigid sequence of routing signals first, power traces second, and ground connections last. For multilayer boards, the stackup and reference planes should be planned before routing begins. High-speed interfaces, sensitive analog circuits, and switching power supplies also require early consideration of critical signal paths and current return paths. In practice, the following approach provides a useful starting point. Step 1: Plan the stackup, reference planes, and grounding strategy. Determine which layers will serve as reference planes, provide continuous reference paths for critical nets wherever possible, and establish a grounding strategy appropriate for the circuit. Step 2: Route critical nets first. These include high-speed differential signals, clock signals, sensitive analog signals, and switching power supply loops with strict current-loop requirements. Such nets often have tighter constraints on routing length, return paths, impedance, or noise coupling. Step 3: Route other power nets. Determine trace widths, copper areas, and routing paths based on operating current, allowable voltage drop, temperature rise, and power integrity requirements. Step 4: Complete ordinary low-speed signal routing. Route signals such as buttons, indicator LEDs, and general-purpose I/O (GPIO) using the remaining routing space while meeting electrical and manufacturing requirements. This is a general guideline rather than a fixed sequence for every PCB. Routing priorities should be adjusted according to circuit topology, component placement, signal edge rates, power levels, and design constraints. For multilayer boards, planning continuous reference planes in advance is generally more important than simply routing all ground connections first. PCB Ground Plane and Return Path Design A ground plane provides a reference for signals and a return path for power and signal currents. Poor ground plane design can increase return-path inductance and loop area, potentially affecting signal integrity, power integrity, and EMC performance. Key Ground Plane Design Principles Prioritize reference plane continuity. For multilayer PCBs, a continuous ground plane should be used as the reference plane for high-speed and sensitive signals wherever possible. Avoid unnecessary ground plane cuts or slots beneath critical traces. Otherwise, return currents may be forced to detour, increasing loop area and the risk of electromagnetic radiation. Choose a grounding strategy based on the circuit. Digital, analog, and power circuits may have different noise and return-current requirements. However, physically separating DGND, AGND, and PGND and connecting them at a single point is not a universal requirement. In many mixed-signal designs, a continuous ground plane combined with careful component placement and current-path management can provide better noise performance. If separate ground regions or single-point connections are necessary, determine the connection strategy based on circuit topology and the component manufacturer's recommendations. Keep critical ground connections short. The ground terminals of decoupling capacitors, return terminals of power devices, and ground connections near interfaces should use low-inductance paths whenever possible. Properly placed ground vias can help reduce parasitic inductance. The number and placement of vias in high-frequency regions should be determined according to current paths, stackup structure, and EMC requirements. Common Ground Plane Design Mistakes For multilayer PCBs, using a continuous ground plane is generally preferable to relying on numerous narrow, manually routed ground traces. For single-layer and double-layer boards, copper pours, trace routing, and component placement should be coordinated to provide continuous, low-impedance return paths for critical nets wherever possible. Common mistakes include: Splitting the ground plane unnecessarily and forcing return currents to take longer paths. Routing critical high-speed signals across ground plane splits or slots. Placing decoupling capacitors too far from power pins or using long ground connections. Leaving unnecessary floating copper areas that introduce parasitic effects. Connecting different ground nets without a clear circuit-level justification. There is no single ground trace width that applies to every PCB. Ground traces carrying significant current should be sized according to current, copper thickness, allowable temperature rise, and voltage drop. For multilayer boards, a ground plane will often provide lower return-path impedance than narrow, manually routed ground traces. Common Failure Analysis Consider an industrial data acquisition board where ordinary signals were routed before the grounding arrangement was fully considered. Several traces fragmented the reference plane in the analog section, affecting the return paths of some sampling signals. During operation, the board exhibited fluctuating measurements and failed to meet the expected EMC performance. Troubleshooting should focus on ground plane continuity, signal return paths, analog and digital component placement, and power supply noise coupling rather than assuming that the routing sequence alone caused the failure. Corrective actions should address the actual failure mechanism and may include rerouting traces, restoring reference plane continuity, or optimizing component placement. Routing Critical Signals and Power Traces High-speed signals, sensitive analog signals, and power circuits have different design constraints. They should be routed according to their electrical characteristics rather than assigned priorities based solely on signal frequency or trace width. High-Speed Signals and Sensitive Analog Signals High-speed differential pairs , clock signals, DDR signals, RF signals, and sensitive analog nets such as ADC inputs often require their routing paths to be considered during the component placement stage. （High-Speed PCB Routing and Differential Pair Design） Control routing length and return paths. Critical nets should avoid unnecessary detours and vias while maintaining a continuous reference plane. Whether a high-speed trace is sufficiently short depends on factors such as signal rise time, propagation delay, and circuit requirements, not just clock frequency. Control impedance and timing. For high-speed interfaces such as USB and HDMI, target impedance, trace width, spacing, and other routing constraints should be determined according to interface specifications and the actual PCB stackup. Differential impedance cannot be determined by trace width alone; dielectric thickness, copper thickness, reference planes, and trace geometry also affect it. For DDR and other timing-sensitive parallel interfaces, length matching should follow the timing budget specified by the component manufacturer rather than applying the same length-matching requirement to every signal. Reduce crosstalk risk. The 3W rule can serve as an initial trace spacing guideline, but it does not guarantee that crosstalk will be eliminated. Actual spacing requirements also depend on parallel routing length, dielectric thickness, signal edge rate, and stackup structure. Signal integrity simulation or testing may be necessary for critical nets. Keep signals away from major noise sources. Sensitive analog traces should be routed away from switching nodes, high-current loops, and other noisy areas whenever possible. For high-speed signals, the need for additional clearance from the board edge or the use of ground via fences should be evaluated according to specific EMC requirements. Ordinary Low-Speed Signal Routing Signals such as buttons, indicator LEDs, and general-purpose I/O typically do not require the same level of impedance control as high-speed interfaces. However, they must still meet electrical and reliability requirements. During routing: Meet minimum trace width, spacing, and manufacturing requirements. Avoid unnecessary detours and densely packed parallel traces. Keep traces away from critical high-speed nets, sensitive analog areas, and high-current power loops. Evaluate crosstalk and EMC risks for low-speed interfaces with fast edge rates or connections to external cables. Ordinary low-speed signals can generally be routed more flexibly, but they should not be treated as nets that only need electrical connectivity. Power Traces and Power Loops Power routing must provide sufficient current-carrying capacity, control voltage drop and temperature rise, and maintain appropriate current paths for critical power circuits. Size traces according to actual requirements. Trace width should be determined by copper thickness, whether the trace is on an outer or inner layer, operating current, allowable temperature rise, and trace length. High-current nets also require evaluation of copper temperature rise, voltage drop, and current density at connection points. A fixed trace-width-to-current table alone is not sufficient to determine whether a design is safe. Minimize critical power loop areas. For switching regulators such as DC-DC converters, prioritize the layout of high-(di/dt) current loops. Keep relevant connections short and follow the IC manufacturer's recommended layout for input bypass capacitors, power devices, and other critical components. This helps reduce parasitic inductance and noise radiation. Control noise coupling. Switching nodes and high-current loops should be kept away from sensitive analog signals and other noise-sensitive nets whenever possible. Spacing between different power rails should be determined by voltage, current, switching noise, and insulation requirements rather than by a blanket rule that all power traces at different voltage levels must be separated. Use decoupling capacitors appropriately. Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as practical to their corresponding power pins and connected to the power and reference planes through low-inductance paths. Capacitance, package size, and capacitor combinations should be selected according to component requirements and power integrity targets. Decoupling capacitors cannot compensate for poor power loop design. Power traces are not always better when made wider. Excessive trace width can consume routing space needed by critical nets. Similarly, inner-layer copper is not inherently worse than outer-layer routing for heat dissipation. The appropriate routing approach depends on current capacity, copper area, heat transfer paths, and stackup structure. A Practical PCB Routing Workflow After the stackup and component placement have been planned, the following workflow provides a useful starting point. The sequence should be adjusted to suit the constraints of each project. Step 1: Plan the stackup, reference planes, and board outline. Define the board outline, keep-out areas, connector positions, and layer functions. Establish the reference planes and grounding strategy for critical nets. Step 2: Complete critical component placement. Position high-speed interface ICs, crystals, ADCs, power ICs, and power devices with consideration for signal paths, power loops, thermal performance, and EMC requirements. Step 3: Route critical nets. Prioritize nets with strict timing, impedance, noise, or return-path constraints. These may include high-speed differential pairs, clock signals, sensitive analog signals, and critical switching power loops. Step 4: Route other power nets. Determine trace widths and routing paths according to current, voltage drop, and temperature rise requirements. Check decoupling capacitor placement and power return paths. Step 5: Complete ordinary signal routing. Route GPIO, buttons, indicator LEDs, and other general-purpose nets while meeting design rules and avoiding unnecessary interference with critical nets. Step 6: Review copper pours and grounding connections. Complete ground pours, check thermal relief connections and ground vias, verify reference plane continuity, and remove unnecessary floating copper. Ensure that copper pours do not compromise return paths for critical nets. Step 7: Run DRC and perform a design review. Check trace width, spacing, vias, impedance constraints, differential pairs, length matching, and manufacturability. For high-speed or high-power designs, perform signal integrity analysis, power integrity analysis, thermal analysis, or EMC validation as appropriate. Common PCB Routing Problems and How to Avoid Them Common Failure 1: Discontinuous Reference Planes Cause EMC Problems On a controller board, high-speed signals were routed across a split in the reference plane to avoid other nets. This increased the distance that return currents had to travel, and high-frequency radiation problems appeared during testing. Such failures should be investigated by examining the routing, reference planes, and test results. Possible corrective actions include rerouting the signals, restoring reference plane continuity, or rearranging components and other nets to reduce return-path discontinuities. Common Failure 2: Digital Noise Interferes with Sensitive Analog Signals An ADC circuit exhibited fluctuating readings. Investigation revealed that the analog input traces were routed close to digital signals and a switching power supply, creating potential noise coupling paths. Optimization should focus on the analog input routing, reference plane, front-end filtering, component placement, and power supply noise. Measurements should be used to confirm the dominant interference source. Only after identifying the failure mechanism should engineers adjust trace spacing, grounding, or filtering. （Common PCB Routing Mistakes and Design Rule Violations） Conclusion Effective PCB routing requires more than electrical connectivity and compliance with design rules. It also involves careful consideration of reference planes, return paths, signal integrity, power integrity, current-carrying capacity, and electromagnetic compatibility. Planning the stackup and critical nets in advance, applying routing strategies appropriate to each circuit, and performing a thorough design review can help reduce design defects, lower rework costs, and improve product reliability. Verify Now Blog > Power Supply Pinout Explained: VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, and BAT Power Supply Pinout Explained: VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, and BAT by: Mila Oct 19,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply pinout power supply pins DC-DC converter pins VIN vs VOUT Isn’t VIN the power input and VOUT the output? Many beginner hardware engineers have this question in PCB layout when they first look at power ICs and power module schematics. If a power supply essentially has an input and an output, why are some pins labeled VIN and VOUT, while others are called SW, PH, or BAT? VIN usually refers to the power input, while VOUT refers to the power output. However, neither label necessarily means the voltage is already regulated. SW/PH typically identifies a switching node in a DC-DC converter, where high-frequency switching waveforms are present. BAT is a battery-related pin whose function and current direction depend on the specific IC. These pins serve different purposes. Don’t treat them as interchangeable just because their names look familiar. （Power Supply Pins Explained） SW and PH Pins: Understanding the Switching Node SW stands for Switch, while PH commonly stands for Phase. In many Buck converters, both names refer to the switching node connected to the power switches and the inductor. The exact meaning still depends on the IC and its datasheet. Take a synchronous Buck converter as an example. When the high-side MOSFET Q1 turns on, SW is pulled close to VIN. When the low-side MOSFET Q2 turns on, SW is pulled close to GND. So SW is neither a conventional DC input nor a regulated output. Instead, it rapidly switches between high and low voltage levels. Under ideal steady-state conditions, the average SW voltage is approximately equal to the output voltage: VOUT ≈ D × VIN Here, D is the duty cycle, or the fraction of each switching period during which SW stays high. In an ideal Buck converter, the IC regulates the output voltage by adjusting the PWM duty cycle. Real circuits also have to account for MOSFET voltage drops, parasitic effects, and other losses. Three things you should know 1. In a typical Buck converter, SW connects to the output through an inductor. The inductor and output capacitor work together to transfer energy and filter the switching waveform, providing a relatively stable DC voltage to the load. SW should not be treated as a conventional regulated output. 2. The SW node of an asynchronous Buck converter may go below ground. When the high-side switch turns off and the inductor current flows through the freewheeling diode, SW may be pulled slightly below GND. The actual negative voltage depends on the diode drop, parasitic effects, and switching transients rather than a fixed value. 3. The SW node has a high dv/dt and is a major source of EMI and ringing. When measuring its waveform, use a short probe ground spring or another suitable low-inductance grounding method. Avoid long probe ground leads, which can introduce additional ringing. SW vs. PH: What’s the Difference? Different manufacturers may use different names for similar switching nodes. In multiphase Buck controllers, each phase typically has its own PH or SW node. The switching waveforms usually share the same switching frequency but are phase-shifted relative to one another, which helps explain why PH is a common label. Single-phase converters often use SW as a more straightforward name for the switching node. However, SW, PH, and even LX are not guaranteed to be interchangeable across every IC. When checking a schematic, the safest approach is to read the Pin Description section of the datasheet and confirm the pin's function and recommended connections. BAT Pin Explained: Three Common Applications The BAT label can be misleading if you assume it means "battery output." In reality, it generally identifies a battery-related connection, and its function and current direction depend on the IC's purpose and internal architecture. （SW vs. VOUT in a Buck Converter） Three common BAT pin applications 1. BAT on a battery charger IC Take the TP4056 as an example. Its BAT pin connects to the positive terminal of the battery. During charging, the IC supplies charging current through this pin and monitors the battery voltage. It is not a general-purpose power output intended for arbitrary loads. 2. BAT in a battery-powered system On some PMICs designed to support battery operation, BAT is the battery connection. The IC can draw power from the battery and supply the system through its internal power conversion or distribution circuitry. The exact function depends on the IC architecture. 3. BAT on a power-path management IC A charger with power-path management, such as the BQ24075, typically provides both BAT and SYS connections. When an adapter is connected, the system can be powered from the input supply while the battery charges. When the adapter is removed, the system can switch to battery power. However, voltage dips and power interruptions during the transition depend on the IC's characteristics, system load, and surrounding circuit design. Not every implementation guarantees a completely seamless switchover under all conditions. Remember this: BAT is a battery-related connection, not a general-purpose output. Whether it connects to the battery or the system depends on the datasheet, not the name alone. VIN vs. VOUT vs. SW: Understanding the Differences When a power module provides VIN and VOUT pins, it usually means that a substantial portion of the power conversion circuitry is integrated into the module. You generally don't need to build the entire power stage externally as you would with a more discrete design. Power module vs. DC-DC converter IC Typical examples include TI's LMZM series, ADI's µModule series, and Murata's OKI-78SR series. These modules integrate some or most of the power conversion circuitry. External components, such as input and output capacitors, are generally all you need to connect according to the datasheet. However, not every device with a VOUT pin is a power module. Some integrated DC-DC converters also provide a VOUT pin. The distinction depends on the internal architecture and pin definitions. Many DC-DC converter ICs that use an external inductor, such as the TPS54331, MP2359, and LMR14030, expose an SW pin. The inductor, output capacitor, and feedback resistors typically need to be designed externally, and some devices also require an external compensation network. This approach offers greater design flexibility, but it also demands more attention to PCB layout, power-stage loops, and EMI control. SW Pin PCB Layout: Copper Area and EMI Considerations You've probably heard that "the SW copper area should be as small as possible." There's a good reason for this advice, but smaller isn't automatically better in every respect. SW is a high-dv/dt node. An unnecessarily large copper area can increase parasitic capacitance and electromagnetic radiation. At the same time, switching current flows through this node, so its copper geometry must also meet current-carrying, thermal, and parasitic requirements. PCB layout comparison of SW nodes A more practical approach is to keep the SW copper area compact while meeting current-carrying and thermal requirements. Avoid unnecessarily large copper pours, but don't compromise electrical or thermal performance just to minimize the area. The high-frequency current loop deserves just as much attention. Place the input bypass capacitor close to the power switching loop to minimize its area. The placement of the SW copper relative to adjacent ground planes should be evaluated based on the stackup, parasitic capacitance, and EMI requirements. Also, keep feedback traces away from noisy nodes such as SW whenever possible. These layout practices can help improve EMI performance and reduce switching waveform ringing. For more practical tips on power supply PCB layout, including switching loop optimization, SW node routing, and grounding, see our guide to DCDC Power PCB Layout Guidelines . Common Power Supply Pins and Their Functions Let's review some of the most common pins you'll encounter on power ICs. Common power supply pin overview COMP deserves special attention. It's easy to mistake COMP for an input, but on power controllers with external compensation, COMP is typically the output of the error amplifier. An RC compensation network may be connected according to the datasheet's recommendations. FB is typically the feedback input. The IC senses the output voltage through this pin, often using a resistor divider, and compares it with an internal reference. PG/PGOOD indicates the power-good status. An open-drain output is common and requires a pull-up resistor as specified in the datasheet, although not all devices use the same output structure. In addition, EN is typically used to enable or disable the IC, while GND/PGND refers to ground or power-ground connections. Follow the recommended grounding arrangement for the specific device. A quick reference table for common power supply pins These are common pin names and functions, not universal definitions. Always refer to the datasheet for the specific device you're using. Power supply pin names are more than just labels. Understanding the functions of VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, BAT, FB, COMP, and PG can help you interpret a circuit more accurately, follow the power flow, and identify potential issues during debugging. Many beginner hardware engineers have this question in PCB layout when they first look at power ICs and power module schematics. If a power supply essentially has an input and an output, why are some pins labeled VIN and VOUT, while others are called SW, PH, or BAT? VIN usually refers to the power input, while VOUT refers to the power output. However, neither label necessarily means the voltage is already regulated. SW/PH typically identifies a switching node in a DC-DC converter, where high-frequency switching waveforms are present. BAT is a battery-related pin whose function and current direction depend on the specific IC. These pins serve different purposes. Don’t treat them as interchangeable just because their names look familiar. （Power Supply Pins Explained） SW and PH Pins: Understanding the Switching Node SW stands for Switch, while PH commonly stands for Phase. In many Buck converters, both names refer to the switching node connected to the power switches and the inductor. The exact meaning still depends on the IC and its datasheet. Take a synchronous Buck converter as an example. When the high-side MOSFET Q1 turns on, SW is pulled close to VIN. When the low-side MOSFET Q2 turns on, SW is pulled close to GND. So SW is neither a conventional DC input nor a regulated output. Instead, it rapidly switches between high and low voltage levels. Under ideal steady-state conditions, the average SW voltage is approximately equal to the output voltage: VOUT ≈ D × VIN Here, D is the duty cycle, or the fraction of each switching period during which SW stays high. In an ideal Buck converter, the IC regulates the output voltage by adjusting the PWM duty cycle. Real circuits also have to account for MOSFET voltage drops, parasitic effects, and other losses. Three things you should know 1. In a typical Buck converter, SW connects to the output through an inductor. The inductor and output capacitor work together to transfer energy and filter the switching waveform, providing a relatively stable DC voltage to the load. SW should not be treated as a conventional regulated output. 2. The SW node of an asynchronous Buck converter may go below ground. When the high-side switch turns off and the inductor current flows through the freewheeling diode, SW may be pulled slightly below GND. The actual negative voltage depends on the diode drop, parasitic effects, and switching transients rather than a fixed value. 3. The SW node has a high dv/dt and is a major source of EMI and ringing. When measuring its waveform, use a short probe ground spring or another suitable low-inductance grounding method. Avoid long probe ground leads, which can introduce additional ringing. SW vs. PH: What’s the Difference? Different manufacturers may use different names for similar switching nodes. In multiphase Buck controllers, each phase typically has its own PH or SW node. The switching waveforms usually share the same switching frequency but are phase-shifted relative to one another, which helps explain why PH is a common label. Single-phase converters often use SW as a more straightforward name for the switching node. However, SW, PH, and even LX are not guaranteed to be interchangeable across every IC. When checking a schematic, the safest approach is to read the Pin Description section of the datasheet and confirm the pin's function and recommended connections. BAT Pin Explained: Three Common Applications The BAT label can be misleading if you assume it means "battery output." In reality, it generally identifies a battery-related connection, and its function and current direction depend on the IC's purpose and internal architecture. （SW vs. VOUT in a Buck Converter） Three common BAT pin applications 1. BAT on a battery charger IC Take the TP4056 as an example. Its BAT pin connects to the positive terminal of the battery. During charging, the IC supplies charging current through this pin and monitors the battery voltage. It is not a general-purpose power output intended for arbitrary loads. 2. BAT in a battery-powered system On some PMICs designed to support battery operation, BAT is the battery connection. The IC can draw power from the battery and supply the system through its internal power conversion or distribution circuitry. The exact function depends on the IC architecture. 3. BAT on a power-path management IC A charger with power-path management, such as the BQ24075, typically provides both BAT and SYS connections. When an adapter is connected, the system can be powered from the input supply while the battery charges. When the adapter is removed, the system can switch to battery power. However, voltage dips and power interruptions during the transition depend on the IC's characteristics, system load, and surrounding circuit design. Not every implementation guarantees a completely seamless switchover under all conditions. Remember this: BAT is a battery-related connection, not a general-purpose output. Whether it connects to the battery or the system depends on the datasheet, not the name alone. VIN vs. VOUT vs. SW: Understanding the Differences When a power module provides VIN and VOUT pins, it usually means that a substantial portion of the power conversion circuitry is integrated into the module. You generally don't need to build the entire power stage externally as you would with a more discrete design. Power module vs. DC-DC converter IC Typical examples include TI's LMZM series, ADI's µModule series, and Murata's OKI-78SR series. These modules integrate some or most of the power conversion circuitry. External components, such as input and output capacitors, are generally all you need to connect according to the datasheet. However, not every device with a VOUT pin is a power module. Some integrated DC-DC converters also provide a VOUT pin. The distinction depends on the internal architecture and pin definitions. Many DC-DC converter ICs that use an external inductor, such as the TPS54331, MP2359, and LMR14030, expose an SW pin. The inductor, output capacitor, and feedback resistors typically need to be designed externally, and some devices also require an external compensation network. This approach offers greater design flexibility, but it also demands more attention to PCB layout, power-stage loops, and EMI control. SW Pin PCB Layout: Copper Area and EMI Considerations You've probably heard that "the SW copper area should be as small as possible." There's a good reason for this advice, but smaller isn't automatically better in every respect. SW is a high-dv/dt node. An unnecessarily large copper area can increase parasitic capacitance and electromagnetic radiation. At the same time, switching current flows through this node, so its copper geometry must also meet current-carrying, thermal, and parasitic requirements. PCB layout comparison of SW nodes A more practical approach is to keep the SW copper area compact while meeting current-carrying and thermal requirements. Avoid unnecessarily large copper pours, but don't compromise electrical or thermal performance just to minimize the area. The high-frequency current loop deserves just as much attention. Place the input bypass capacitor close to the power switching loop to minimize its area. The placement of the SW copper relative to adjacent ground planes should be evaluated based on the stackup, parasitic capacitance, and EMI requirements. Also, keep feedback traces away from noisy nodes such as SW whenever possible. These layout practices can help improve EMI performance and reduce switching waveform ringing. For more practical tips on power supply PCB layout, including switching loop optimization, SW node routing, and grounding, see our guide to DCDC Power PCB Layout Guidelines . Common Power Supply Pins and Their Functions Let's review some of the most common pins you'll encounter on power ICs. Common power supply pin overview COMP deserves special attention. It's easy to mistake COMP for an input, but on power controllers with external compensation, COMP is typically the output of the error amplifier. An RC compensation network may be connected according to the datasheet's recommendations. FB is typically the feedback input. The IC senses the output voltage through this pin, often using a resistor divider, and compares it with an internal reference. PG/PGOOD indicates the power-good status. An open-drain output is common and requires a pull-up resistor as specified in the datasheet, although not all devices use the same output structure. In addition, EN is typically used to enable or disable the IC, while GND/PGND refers to ground or power-ground connections. Follow the recommended grounding arrangement for the specific device. Power supply pin names are more than just labels. Verify Now Blog > Reflow Soldering vs. Wave Soldering: Key Differences and PCB Design Tips Reflow Soldering vs. Wave Soldering: Key Differences and PCB Design Tips by: Mila Oct 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout Reflow Soldering Wave Soldering SMT vs. THT PCB Assembly PCB Soldering As hardware engineers, we design the PCB, select the components, and send the Gerber files to the manufacturer. But have you ever wondered why some components go through reflow soldering while others require wave soldering? Both processes melt solder to form electrical and mechanical connections, so why does a production line need two different types of equipment? The reason is not that equipment manufacturers are making the process unnecessarily complicated. The main difference between reflow soldering and wave soldering lies in how the solder reaches the joints and which types of components each process is best suited for. For hardware engineers, understanding these two processes is more than just useful knowledge. It can affect PCB layout , component selection, pad design, and even troubleshooting during manufacturing. How Reflow Soldering Works Reflow soldering is primarily used for surface-mount technology (SMT) components, such as resistors, capacitors, SOPs, QFNs, and BGAs. The basic process is straightforward: solder paste is first printed onto the PCB pads, and the components are then placed on the board. Next, the PCB assembly passes through a reflow oven, where the solder paste goes through several stages, including preheating, heating, time above the liquidus temperature, and cooling. These stages allow the solder to melt, wet the surfaces, and solidify to form reliable joints. One detail that is easy to overlook is that reflow soldering is not simply about heating the entire PCB to a fixed temperature. The temperature profile over time must be carefully controlled. Taking the common SAC305 lead-free solder alloy as an example, its melting range is approximately 217–220°C. During reflow, the solder joint temperature must rise above the liquidus temperature and remain there for a certain period. However, the peak temperature, time above liquidus, and heating and cooling rates depend on factors such as the solder paste, component temperature limits, and PCB thermal mass. These parameters cannot be applied universally to every board. （reflow soldering） How Wave Soldering Works Imagine a PCB with small resistors, large connectors, and power pads connected to extensive copper areas. Small components generally have lower thermal mass and heat up quickly, while large components and pads absorb more heat and may heat up more slowly. If the temperature rises too quickly, the small components may approach their peak temperature before the solder on the larger pads has fully melted. On the other hand, increasing the peak temperature too much or extending the time at high temperatures to accommodate the larger pads can increase thermal stress on components, damage the PCB, and raise the risk of solder oxidation. The real challenge of reflow soldering is to ensure that every solder joint receives enough heat, but not excessive heat, while staying within the temperature limits of the components. （wave soldering） Why Reflow Temperature Control Matters Wave soldering works in a more straightforward way. The equipment melts the solder and uses a pump to create a stable wave of molten solder. After the PCB passes through flux application and preheating, its solder side comes into contact with the molten solder. The solder wets the component leads and PCB pads, forming the joints. Traditional wave soldering is most commonly used for through-hole technology (THT) components, such as through-hole connectors, transformers, relay sockets, and some power components. Their leads pass through holes in the PCB, allowing the molten solder to contact the leads and pads from the solder side and form reliable joints. Why Wave Soldering Isn't Suitable for Every PCB Wave soldering brings molten solder into direct contact with the solder side of the PCB. If the board contains a large number of surface-mount components, especially fine-pitch leads or packages with bottom-side pads, solder may bridge adjacent leads or cause soldering defects in components that are unsuitable for this process. However, this does not mean that surface-mount components can never be wave soldered. When wave soldering is used for suitable SMT components, the component orientation, pad spacing, and solder mask design must be considered carefully. In some cases, adhesive is also used to hold the components in place during soldering. PCB travel direction, protruding lead length, and component placement on the solder side must also be taken into account. If the design is unsuitable, even well-adjusted equipment parameters may not be enough to ensure consistent production quality. It is worth noting that reflow soldering is not limited to surface-mount components, nor is wave soldering restricted to through-hole components. Other processes, including selective wave soldering and pin-in-paste soldering (also known as intrusive reflow soldering), are used in actual manufacturing. The appropriate method depends on package structures, component distribution, solder joint reliability, and production requirements. （PCB Assembly） PCB Design Considerations for Reflow and Wave Soldering 1. Component and Pad Design For SMT packages such as QFNs and BGAs, engineers need to consider pad dimensions, solder paste printing, stencil design, and the reflow temperature profile. For through-hole components, important factors include hole diameter, copper thickness, lead dimensions, and solder fill. Package and pad design affect not only electrical performance but also soldering quality during PCB assembly. 2. Copper Distribution and Thermal Management When a power component's pad is connected to a large copper area, the copper can absorb and distribute heat, making it more difficult for the local pad to reach the required temperature. This may prevent the solder from melting sufficiently. During design, engineers should evaluate copper distribution, pad structure, and the actual temperature profile rather than simply increasing the oven temperature to compensate. 3. Common Soldering Defects and Their Causes For example, tombstoning of resistors after reflow soldering may result from uneven heating between the two pads, differences in solder paste volume, or component placement errors. Solder bridging between connector leads after wave soldering may be related to pad spacing, lead orientation, flux application, or wave parameters. When these defects occur, engineers should investigate the PCB design and soldering process alongside the components themselves. Hardware engineers do not necessarily need to operate soldering equipment themselves, but they should understand how their designs affect manufacturability. Reflow soldering focuses on controlling the temperature profile during solder paste melting, while wave soldering focuses on controlling the contact between molten solder and the PCB's solder side. Neither process is universally better than the other. The right choice depends on component packages, PCB layout, and production requirements. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity.
