events.before: Resources Case Studies Case Study: NASA Partners with Xometry to Fast-track Critical Life Support Systems on the International Space Station Case Study: NASA Partners with Xometry to Fast-track Critical Life Support Systems on the International Space Station Written by Serena Ngoh 4 min read Published October 9, 2020 NASA engineers at the Marshall Space Flight Center employed Xometry’s large format CNC machining capabilities to build mission-critical air purification units. At a Glance Industry Manufacturing Services Utilized Project Brief Solution Industry ☑ Aerospace & Defense ☐ Automotive ☐ Consumer Products ☐ Education ☐ Electronics and Semiconductors ☐ Energy ☐ Industrial ☐ Medical & Dental ☐ Robotics ☐ Supply Chain & Purchasing Manufacturing Services Utilized ☑ CNC Machining ☐ Sheet Metal Fabrication ☐ 3D Printing ☐ Urethane Casting ☐ Injection Molding ☐ Die Casting and Extrusion ☑ Post-Processing ☑ Inspection Services Project Brief NASA needed to fast-track the production of components for an air purification unit for the International Space Station. Expedited manufacturing would help the team remain on its proposed rocket launch schedule. Solution Xometry sourced uncommonly large stock material and CNC machined 2 single body vessels with extremely tight tolerances and critical sealing surfaces—all within a 4-week lead time. Xometry reduced the projected lead time by 2 months and decreased costs by 75%, enabling future flexible and comprehensive design methodologies. What Do You Need to Live In Space? Recyclable Energy Systems. On the International Space Station (ISS), critical resources are maintained in closed-loop systems. These systems replenish resources such as oxygen and water, which allows NASA astronauts to live 220 miles (350 km) above the earth. The design, fabrication, and maintenance of these systems is the job of NASA’s Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) team. The latest project that ECLSS engineers at the Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) in Huntsville, Alabama, are working on is an air purification unit that will scrub carbon dioxide from the air via a desiccant (a material that draws water from air) and a molecular sieve (a material that traps and expels carbon dioxide molecules outside the space station). This system is known as the Four Bed Carbon Dioxide Scrubber (4BCO2) system. The Challenge: Building Extra Large Flight Components at Record Speeds Over the last 2 years, the design of the 4BCO2 system has progressed using a multi-part design for the cylindrical bed hardware. This design required the parts to be welded together. As the manufacturing process began on the cylindrical beds—the foundational components of the system—ECLSS engineers ran into a problem. It was determined that the welding operations (the best method for NASA’s in-house capabilities), would introduce delays due to a lengthy weld certification process. This posed significant risk to the team’s ability to meet their hardware delivery schedule. Due the schedule risk, the ECLSS team decided to abandon the welded design and associated weld certification process and explore other design options. Redesigning the parts by reducing the size of the beds was not an option as it would compromise the system’s functional performance. Instead, the team decided on a one-piece barrel design. This decision required the fabrication to be outsourced in order to get the priority needed to maintain schedule. The 4BCO2 team, led by NASA engineer Jimmy Hill, reached out to Xometry to see if the company could handle this highly custom job. CAD assembly of the air purification units “Xometry’s supplier management passes savings on to us. Parts are so fast and cheap that we can change the way we work and design.” Jimmy Hill Lead mechanical design engineer at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center A Highly Custom CNC Machining Solution Hill spoke with Xometry’s dedicated account representatives about the project requirements and timeline, emphasizing that the project was now behind schedule. Hill requested a 4-week turnaround, which would involve sourcing a specialized, large-format CNC machine shop in Xometry’s ITAR-certified network. Within the allotted 4 weeks, Xometry secured rare, specialty heat-treated, cylindrical aluminum stock as well as a Manufacturing Partner to make the 12” by 16” diameter parts. The parts were carefully machined to aerospace standards, including tight tolerances of 0.005” and accuracy to GD&T. Critical sealing surfaces of the pressure vessel were machined with o-ring grooves, close-fitting parts, tight side and positional control tolerances, and highly accurate tapped and thru-holes. The Xometry inspection team verified the parts via CMM inspection before passing the parts on to NASA for the verification testing process. From there, the parts passed all of NASA’s individual material tests as well as the full integration tests. “We asked for a lot, and Xometry did an amazing job. Your CNC machining service saved the day.” Jimmy Hill Lead mechanical design engineer at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center Xometry CNC machined 4 vessel components to make 2 air purification units for the NASA International Space Station Xometry has a video version of this case study. Watch It Now Xometry Manufacturing Is Changing the Way NASA Develops Parts With help from Xometry’s on-demand manufacturing services, the air purification unit developed by NASA’s ECLSS team is on track to go up in the Cygnus rocket during the NG-15 launch in 2021. Xometry’s turnkey services reduced what would have been a 3-month in-house production timeline to just one month, preventing a domino effect of delays. Hill says that Xometry’s market-accurate pricing and supplier management allows NASA to save 3-4 times the projected cost of in-house manufacturing. And because of the high-cost savings, the team’s development methodology can shift from linear prototyping to a more lean, parallel prototyping methodology. This has the effect of dramatically reducing project lead times. “We typically have a lot of internal overhead with paperwork and personnel costs, but Xometry’s time-saving supplier management passes on savings to us. Xometry has capabilities that we don’t have in-house, and is so fast and cheap that we don’t mind paying for 2 or 3 [flight equivalent] versions at once. This helps us gain time in our schedule,” says Hill. With the success of the air purification unit and various other jobs, NASA teams across 10 US facilities are confident that Xometry can take on mission-critical work for all types of machined, sheet metal, or 3D printed parts. “Because of Xometry’s flexibility, speed, and quality, all of our projects now look to Xometry for cost effective supply of space flight hardware for life support systems.” David Jones ECLSS Integration & Development Lead at Marshall Space Flight Center Serena Ngoh I write about Xometry and all things manufacturing. You might also see me hosting webinars, designing infographics, producing videos, and working directly with customers to tell their manufacturing success stories. events.before: Resources Case Studies Case Study: From Workshop to Moonshot – Xometry's Role in Intuitive Machines' Lunar Return Case Study: From Workshop to Moonshot – Xometry's Role in Intuitive Machines' Lunar Return Written by Nathan Miller 7 min read Published May 7, 2024 Learn how Xometry provided mission-critical CNC machined parts for Intuitive Machines’ lunar lander, Odysseus, helping its engineering team stay on schedule and achieve the first successful American Moon landing in over 50 years. Industries Manufacturing Services Utilized Project Brief Solution Industries Aerospace Manufacturing Services Utilized CNC machining Project Brief NASA tasked Intuitive Machines with building a lunar lander, dubbed Odysseus, that would make the first successful American landing on the Moon since Apollo 17. To meet their fast-approaching deadline, they needed to source hundreds of specialized machined parts quickly. Solution By working with Xometry, Intuitive Machines was able to source hundreds of primer-coated CNC machined parts that held the craft together as it made its descent to the lunar surface. Odysseus touched down safely, began transmitting valuable data to NASA, and helped establish a hopeful precedent for the future of commercial space exploration. Odysseus Sticks the (Lunar) Landing On the evening of February 22, 2024, the Intuitive Machines team waited to see if Odysseus, the lunar lander they spent years building together, had survived its harrowing journey to the Moon’s surface. “On landing day, we were all huddled up out there in the shop staring at the timer – we knew it was going be landing in a couple of minutes,” said Brandon Crain, a procurement manager for Intuitive Machines. Intuitive Machines is a diversified space exploration company focused on pioneering the commercial landscape of outer space and is part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative . The science and technology payloads sent to the Moon’s surface as part of CLPS are helping lay the foundation for future human missions and a sustainable human presence on the lunar surface. After Odysseus landed, the group continued to wait anxiously. “It's just crickets. Nothing. We're all just waiting,” Crain said. “It was like 10 minutes where we're all wondering, ‘Did it work?’” Credit: Intuitive Machines/ Nick Rios Tim Crain (no relation), chief technology officer at Intuitive Machines, finally shared the news the team was waiting to hear “Alright, guys, we can confirm without a doubt that our hardware is on the surface of the Moon.” The Intuitive Machines team was able to successfully land the Company’s Nova-C class lunar lander on the Moon, marking the United States’ first lunar landing since Apollo 17 more than 50 years ago. “The minute that they could confirm that they had a signal, the place went nuts – it was amazing! Because until that minute, we didn't know [if it survived the landing],” Crain recalled, smiling. “That was a very, very fun night.” For most, Odysseus’ journey began with a rocket launch and ended with a successful landing. For Crain and his team, that night was an exhilarating conclusion to years of hard work and dedication. To the Moon or Bust Credit: Intuitive Machines/ Nick Rios Brandon Crain serves as a liaison between the engineering and purchasing teams at Intuitive Machines. “Once the engineers have parts they need made, they hand them off to me. I facilitate which part comes from where and I find the right vendor for each one.” Crain first became familiar with the company by working with them as a vendor himself. When the leaders at Intuitive Machines learned of his 25 years of experience sourcing custom-machined components, they hired him as a full-time member of the team. When Crain joined the Intuitive Machines team, he set out to refine their procurement process. The 150 engineers in his Houston-based team had grown accustomed to ordering parts on their own without going through a vendor vetting process. When looking at their vendor orders, he often asked, “Is this even something this person should be selling us? Are they qualified to make this type of part? How are they going to inspect it?” Crain said. Thankfully, Crain knew from experiences in his previous role that he could turn to Xometry to help simplify the procurement process. “Xometry quickly helped me plug some gaps. [With Xometry], we can check boxes for inspections or rely on them if we need additional surface treatments or tight tolerances. The website for submitting quotes is super straightforward. It was an easy way for us to start fixing [these issues] and get stuff very quickly.” Credit: Intuitive Machines/ Nick Rios One afternoon, Crain received a phone call from Xometry’s CEO, Randy Altschuler. “He's said, ‘Hey, I’m seeing a lot of activity on your account – is there anything that you need us to work on?’ I was like, ‘Man, I'm so glad you called me.’ He put some people in place to really help streamline a lot of the issues that we were facing.” Xometry’s applications engineering team helped Crain further streamline the process. “They understood our internal language and helped get things reliably and quickly,” he said. "Xometry’s team was diligent about referencing our internal inventory tracking numbers in their communications. By doing this, Xometry helped us track and resolve DFM issues much more efficiently – which is very helpful when you are tracking hundreds of parts among hundreds of engineers." How Xometry’s CNC Machined Parts Helped Bring Odysseus to the Moon Credit: Intuitive Machines The lunar lander is encased in carbon fiber and aluminum honeycomb sandwich panels. This design makes Odysseus robust enough to withstand landing forces while remaining lightweight. “Mass is the enemy,” Crain explained. “Because the heavier you are, the more fuel you need. The more fuel you need, the heavier you get. And so we do everything we can to be as light as possible while keeping it strong enough for its application.” Unfortunately, while this panel design kept the design lightweight, it did create a challenge for Intuitive Machine’s engineering team. “You can't screw anything into it; It doesn't have the meat,” Crain said “And so anywhere we need a fastener like a screw or bolt, you have to put a metallic body inside of that panel.” By placing Xomery CNC machined spool fittings on each side of the panel, Intuitive Machines’ engineering team was able to create a thread point that they could screw into. These titanium spool fittings are about an inch in diameter and are coated in a special adhesive primer, which helps the spool fasteners bind the panels together. Credit: Intuitive Machines/ Nick Rios “There are hundreds of those, and they're literally all over the vehicle,” Crain remarked. “[There is a] very good chance that if it got bolted onto the lander, it was bolted through a Xometry spool fastener.” Xometry is equipped with thousands of material and surface finish options. If you don’t see what you need on our menu, that doesn’t mean Xometry can’t source it. Select “Other,” and our DFM team will get back to you with the price and lead times. Xometry will match you with a supplier that is best suited to your unique needs. In the rare circumstance where Xometry does not have immediate access to a material or finish option, it will onboard suppliers with materials or finishes you provide. When he brought the issue to Xometry, “they took on that custom primer for us,” Crain said. “And it's been a game changer for building the first vehicle. We ordered hundreds of parts with that primer on it, and they're on the Moon right now.” One of Crain’s favorite Xometry parts was the CNC machined landing gears designed to make first contact with the lunar surface. After ordering the custom aluminum panels that were placed on the bottom side of the landing gear, Intuitive Machines leadership etched the names of their team into them. “Xometry made and delivered that dish. That was pretty dang cool.” Without Xometry playing the role they did, I don't think we could have put this first lunar lander together in the timeline that we needed to. Xometry’s performance was extremely good, They managed their systems, team, and resources to get us what we needed on time – We knew we could count on them. Brandon Crain Procurement Manager at Intuitive Machines If you're ready to start your next project, we’d love to help. Get an instant quote today, or connect with a member of our team . Building the Next Generation of Moon Landers With Xometry’s Support Credit: Intuitive Machines/ Carter Pytel After successfully landing its first spacecraft, Intuitive Machines has fundamentally disrupted the economics of landing on the Moon through a fixed-price performance contract, demonstrating unprecedented economics and efficiency to commercial customers and NASA. Intuitive Machines is now readying itself for the IM-2 mission. The commercial and NASA payloads on IM-2 complement the pursuit of water on the Moon and the effort to establish a foothold on the south pole, where NASA’s $93 billion Artemis campaign is targeting human missions this decade. Intuitive Machines is assembling IM-2’s propulsion and structural components in-house and will be completing the integration of NASA’s ice mining drill in the fourth quarter of 2024. In addition, Intuitive Machines’ Micro Nova hopper, designed to search for water ice in permanently shaded regions of the Moon, completed thermal vacuum chamber testing before the end of the year. Xometry is excited to support them as they embark on their next voyage into the final frontier. To learn more about how to get the most value from our proprietary platform, be sure to watch 7 Pro Tips for Mastering Xometry’s Instant Quoting Engine® . This webinar recording is a must-listen for engineering, product design, and procurement professionals looking to leverage Xometry's platform for enhanced manufacturing efficiency. Intuitive Machines is a diversified space exploration company focused on pioneering the commercial landscape of outer space and is part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative . The science and technology payloads sent to the Moon’s surface as part of CLPS are helping lay the foundation for future human missions and a sustainable human presence on the lunar surface. After Odysseus landed, the group continued to wait anxiously. “It's just crickets. Nothing. Because until that minute, we didn't know [if it survived the landing],” Crain recalled, smiling. “That was a very, very fun night.” For most, Odysseus’ journey began with a rocket launch and ended with a successful landing. For Crain and his team, that night was an exhilarating conclusion to years of hard work and dedication. To the Moon or Bust Credit: Intuitive Machines/ Nick Rios Brandon Crain serves as a liaison between the engineering and purchasing teams at Intuitive Machines. “Once the engineers have parts they need made, they hand them off to me. I facilitate which part comes from where and I find the right vendor for each one.” Crain first became familiar with the company by working with them as a vendor himself. When the leaders at Intuitive Machines learned of his 25 years of experience sourcing custom-machined components, they hired him as a full-time member of the team. When Crain joined the Intuitive Machines team, he set out to refine their procurement process. The 150 engineers in his Houston-based team had grown accustomed to ordering parts on their own without going through a vendor vetting process. When looking at their vendor orders, he often asked, “Is this even something this person should be selling us? Are they qualified to make this type of part? How are they going to inspect it?” Crain said. Thankfully, Crain knew from experiences in his previous role that he could turn to Xometry to help simplify the procurement process. “Xometry quickly helped me plug some gaps. [With Xometry], we can check boxes for inspections or rely on them if we need additional surface treatments or tight tolerances. The website for submitting quotes is super straightforward. It was an easy way for us to start fixing [these issues] and get stuff very quickly.” Credit: Intuitive Machines/ Nick Rios One afternoon, Crain received a phone call from Xometry’s CEO, Randy Altschuler. “He's said, ‘Hey, I’m seeing a lot of activity on your account – is there anything that you need us to work on?’ I was like, ‘Man, I'm so glad you called me.’ He put some people in place to really help streamline a lot of the issues that we were facing.” Xometry’s applications engineering team helped Crain further streamline the process. “They understood our internal language and helped get things reliably and quickly,” he said. events.before: Resources Case Studies Case Study: Xometry’s Precise Laser Tube Cutting Helps Sea Box Build, Scale Up a Big Project for a Defense Customer Case Study: Xometry’s Precise Laser Tube Cutting Helps Sea Box Build, Scale Up a Big Project for a Defense Customer Written by Tricia Contreras 7 min read Published September 27, 2024 Learn how this New Jersey-based small business utilized Xometry’s sheet cutting and laser tube cutting services to build a custom structure from the ground up and quickly scale up production. Industries Manufacturing Services Utilized Project Brief Solution Industries ISO containers and modular buildings for commercial and military customers Manufacturing Services Utilized Sheet cutting and laser tube cutting Project Brief Sea Box relies on its in-house engineers and manufacturers for many of its builds, but a large project on a tight timeline required more parts than they could make in-house. Solution The company turned to Xometry to provide the steel sheet metal and tube components for the ground-up build. Since 1984, Sea Box has designed, customized, and manufactured ISO containers and modular buildings for commercial and military applications. From ready-made containers for storage and shipping to custom-built structures for uses ranging from residential to medical, the New Jersey-based small business has expanded its offerings and workforce over the years. Today, it employs about 350 people, including a team of engineers who design unique solutions to fit customers’ needs. Sea Box designs and manufactures modular buildings that are customizable, connectable, and stackable. (Image Credit: Sea Box) Many of Sea Box’s projects are designed and manufactured in-house, but sometimes a large project requires the company to outsource some of the manufacturing. That was the case for a recent project for a defense customer that needed a custom-built prototype on a short timeline. “The schedule and the sheer number of parts required us to reach outside our normal networks and look for other options,” said Jeff Lucas, a senior project manager at Sea Box. Some of Lucas’ colleagues at Sea Box had used Xometry before to get quotes and place orders for custom parts, and they recommended it as a solution for his project. Lucas needed to order roughly 400 machined parts, including sheet metal and laser-cut tubes, so “instead of going to a shop that specializes in sheet metal and another shop that specializes in just tube cutting, we sent everything we needed over,” Lucas said of Xometry. “It was a one-stop shop.” Instead of going to a shop that specializes in sheet metal and another shop that specializes in just tube cutting, we sent everything we needed over [to Xometry]. It was a one-stop shop. Jeff Lucas Senior Project Manager, Sea Box Building From the Ground Up “For most projects, we start with an existing container, and then we modify that,” Lucas said. “For this project, we built it from the ground up, which required specialty tubes and a whole lot more work, because every single piece of the entire build had to be designed, made and purchased, versus just starting with a container, cutting out the corrugated walls and putting in some framing. Additionally, the tolerances that were required on this project were very, very tight—not quite aerospace, but pretty tight—and so the machining capability and the machine work had to be pretty tight.” With such a detailed design, Lucas knew the project would be complicated to schedule since all the parts would need to arrive in a specific order. Sea Box ordered about 400 machined parts, including sheet metal and laser-cut tubes, from Xometry for a ground-up build for a defense customer. (Image Credit: Sea Box) “Trying to schedule all of them and determine lead times is a major driver of our schedule because we can't build anything if we don't have parts here,” he said. Uploading parts to Xometry and being able to track everything on the Teamspace Dashboard simplified the project by giving Lucas and his team an organized source of information. “Being able to look at a full quote for all the parts, and then being able to pick the lead time that worked with our our schedule made it very easy,” he said. “Anytime a part would ship, we would get a notification and the tracking number. We could go on to the project dashboard and see the status of everything that we've ordered, which is very valuable, being able to track that and have access to certification documents and packing slips and whatever other inspection documents we required. In our particular case, we had some parts that were ITAR, so being able to handle the ITAR stuff as well was a major plus. Everything's kind of at your fingertips. Some of the old-school machine shops don't have that sort of tech.” “Being able to look at a full quote for all the parts, and then being able to pick the lead time that worked with our our schedule made it very easy. Anytime a part would ship, we would get a notification and the tracking number. We could go on to the project dashboard and see the status of everything that we've ordered, which is very valuable. Jeff Lucas Senior Project Manager, Sea Box Tight Tolerances Call for Laser Precision Laser-cut tubes were an integral part of the project because “the tubes make up the full structure of this particular container,” Lucas said. “Shipping containers are held to an ISO standard for size and tolerance, so right off the bat, we have to be able to hold those tolerances. But further, for our customers’ equipment to fit, to meet the ISO standards for tolerances on the ultimate size of the container, and for form, fit, and function, ultimately, these tubes have to be the size, and they have to be held within the tolerances that we require. If they're not, there's one or two things that happen. One is we either have to fix the part or replace the part, which is going to drive the schedule down and drive the cost up because we’ve got to re-make it or re-buy it. Or two, it goes in and ultimately, you end up with something else that ends up being out of tolerance, and that impacts our customers’ integration.” Laser-cut tubes ordered from Xometry were an integral part of this Sea Box project. (Image Credit: Sea Box) For some parts of the project that didn’t have such tight tolerances, Lucas’ team ordered tube steel cut to length directly from the steel mill, knowing they could grind off any excess in-house. But for the parts that needed to be perfectly to spec, the team turned to the laser tube cutting capabilities from Xometry. With Xometry parts, “we can have confidence that they're going to be within the tolerances, they're going to be the material they need to be, and they're going to fit the first time without having to rework any part of the job,” he said. Xometry Has the Laser Tube Cutting Solutions You Need for Your Next Project Xometry offers an extensive range of laser tube cutting services . Laser types utilized include fiber laser or CO2 lasers, depending upon the material and application, allowing for very tight tolerances and the ability to cut through wall thicknesses up to 1/2“ on round, square, or rectangular tubes. We now offer instant quotes for tube cutting and tube bending through the Xometry Instant Quoting Engine®, so it’s simpler than ever to get a quote for your next project. Scaling Up for the Future In addition to the ease of ordering parts and his confidence in knowing they would arrive on time, Lucas credits Xometry with making it easy to reorder parts. Repeating or scaling up a project is simple since “all the parts and all the quotes from the prototype were still in the Xometry database,” he said. “So when a customer says, ‘Hey, we're looking for five more, how fast can you do it?’ I can say [to Xometry], ‘Take everything we already did, multiply it by five and give us the pricing, lead time, and all that stuff,” Lucas said. His team did exactly that after the customer approved the prototype and wanted to scale up the project into production. “For all the different parts, we were able to select the lead times that we were looking for. So for parts that we didn't need until a little bit later in the build, we brought them in later, which obviously had an impact on the cost, and we were able to use the money saved on some of that to expedite the parts we needed earlier. So we were able to get started on our build much earlier than anticipated…We issued something like 10 or 11 different purchase orders, and every single one was on time, so there were no late shipments and we haven't had to rework anything, so we were able to go right into production, which was excellent.” Lucas credits Xometry with keeping the project on track and helping Sea Box be able to scale it up for the future. “We wouldn't have been able to pull this job off in the time frame or even on budget [without Xometry,]” he said. Once this low-rate production run of five units is complete, Sea Box plans to scale up production further in 2025. Part of that effort may include augmenting its order with Xometry to include more parts that are pre-assembled, rather than ordered as separate components and welded together onsite. This change could equate to even more time savings that Sea Box could pass along to their customer. “We wouldn't have been able to pull this job off in the time frame or even on budget [without Xometry]. Jeff Lucas Senior Project Manager, Sea Box Tricia Contreras Tricia is a Senior Content Strategist at Xometry. events.before: Resources Case Studies How SentriLock Overcame Supply Chain Disruption with Prototype-to-Production Support How SentriLock Overcame Supply Chain Disruption with Prototype-to-Production Support Written by Tricia Contreras 3 min read Published August 27, 2025 Xometry’s partnership enabled SentriLock to overcome urgent supply constraints, establish a robust onshore manufacturing process, and achieve measurable gains in cost efficiency and production output. When SentriLock , a leader in real estate lockbox solutions, experienced a critical supply chain disruption, the company turned a business challenge into an opportunity for innovation and operational improvement through a partnership with Xometry. The Challenge: When Supply Chains Break Down SentriLock is a real estate management platform known for its innovative electronic lockboxes that give agents flexible access to properties via codes or the SentriKey® app. As a leader in the industry, SentriLock continually invests in product improvements to maintain its competitive edge and deliver exceptional value to its users. However, the company’s initiative to onshore its manufacturing operations hit a major snag when onshoring a redesign of the lockbox key bin failed validation. The Solution: Prototype-to-Production Partnership With limited time to rework the design and find new suppliers, SentriLock engaged Xometry for support in redesign, prototyping, and scaling domestic production. Will Kefauver, SentriLock’s senior lead product development engineer at the time, explained: “I couldn't have done this without the robustness of Xometry’s partner network. I had a certain budget that had to be met. I had target pricing. And what I really loved about Xometry was I could share those parameters with them and ask, ‘How close can you get?’” Xometry leveraged its extensive supplier network and manufacturing technology to: Use additive manufacturing for initial prototyping and design validation Transition to urethane casting for an efficient ramp-up to full-scale tooling Minimize lead times and support rapid design iteration It is unusual to have the good fortune of lower cost, higher availability, simplified assembly, better reliability and increased production throughput in one part change. You certainly shoot for that, but it is rare to have everything come together where you hit every goal. Xometry was a great partner in working closely with SentriLock’s engineering team to deliver these great results. Scott Fisher CEO, SentriLock Seamless Logistics Support To prevent assembly line downtime, Xometry coordinated a creative logistics solution. Based on the budget requirements, Xometry presented a solution to have the tooling made in China. The process involved manufacturing two months’ worth of injection-molded plastic parts in China, which were air-freighted to the U.S., ensuring continued assembly operations. The injection molding tool itself was then ocean-freighted for setup in the U.S., supporting the transition to domestic production. With all these moving parts, streamlined communication played a crucial role. SentriLock worked through a single point of contact at Xometry, eliminating the miscommunication that can come from using multiple vendors. “I would have had to talk to at least six other vendors if it wasn't for Xometry. The fact that I had just one point of contact made it much more efficient for me,” Kefauver said. Achieving Results: Cost Savings and Increased Production By redesigning the key bin with fewer components and onshoring production, SentriLock achieved significant improvements: 25% reduction in part count, resulting in annual material savings of $780,000 Fewer assembly steps, doubling lockbox production from 700 to 1,300 units daily Scott Fisher, CEO of SentriLock, said: “It is unusual to have the good fortune of lower cost, higher availability, simplified assembly, better reliability and increased production throughput in one part change. You certainly shoot for that, but it is rare to have everything come together where you hit every goal. Xometry was a great partner in working closely with SentriLock’s engineering team to deliver these great results." Tricia Contreras Tricia is a Senior Content Strategist at Xometry. Colocation Data Center arrangements give organizations access to power, cooling, physical security, and network connections without owning the building. The host facility supplies redundant power feeds and climate control systems that keep housed servers running without interruption. Network carriers inside the building deliver multiple internet paths, reducing downtime caused by a single connection failure. Trained personnel monitor the premises around the clock to limit unauthorized access to equipment racks. Colocation facilities support Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining operations through stable power delivery and low-latency network links that keep production software running. Manufacturing plants running CNC equipment depend on continuous power and fast data transfer to avoid production halts. Colocation providers reduce capital spending on power, cooling, and security systems since machining facilities lease ready-made space. Scalable rack space lets manufacturing operations add equipment without long construction timelines. Professional-grade security and redundant power feeds stand among the core advantages of colocation arrangements. What Is a Colocation Data Center? A colocation data center is a facility where businesses house owned servers and equipment inside space leased from a specialized provider. The provider supplies power, cooling, physical security, and network connectivity, while companies retain full ownership of the hardware. Companies install, configure, and maintain their own servers. The facility delivers surrounding resources that keep the equipment running. Rack space, redundant power feeds, and monitored access form the resources the facility supplies to housed equipment. Service-level agreements outline uptime guarantees and response times for facility support staff. Information technology operations gain reliability when housed equipment receives redundant power, cooling, and network paths inside a colocation facility. Businesses avoid building private data centers. Equipment costs tend to drop since companies share facility resources across tenants. Downtime risk decreases as monitored power feeds and network links keep critical systems running without interruption. Scalable rack space lets organizations add servers without funding new construction or facility upgrades. Predictable monthly fees replace large upfront capital spending tied to private server rooms. How Does Data Center Colocation Work? Data center colocation works by renting rack space inside a shared facility for customer-owned servers and equipment. The facility supplies power, cooling, and network connectivity while customers retain full control of installed hardware. Businesses manage and configure their own servers, and the provider maintains the surrounding power and cooling systems. Redundant power feeds and monitored cooling reduce equipment failure risk across operating hours. Operational efficiency increases as predictable resource delivery lowers maintenance demands on internal staff. Service agreements define uptime targets and response times for facility support teams. Companies scale capacity by adding servers without funding new construction projects. Reliability improves through redundant connections and trained personnel monitoring the facility around the clock. Reduced downtime and lower upfront spending stand among the primary results of the colocation model. Predictable monthly fees replace large capital investments tied to private server rooms. How Does a Data Center Support Colocation Services? A data center supports colocation services through physical building systems and operational support teams. The facility creates a secure environment for housed equipment, and trained staff monitor access around the clock. Power systems are maintained through redundant feeds and backup generators that prevent service interruptions. Network access remains available through multiple carrier connections routed into the building. Equipment stays protected behind locked cages, biometric checkpoints, and continuous video monitoring. Service continuity improves as redundant systems reduce the risk of unplanned outages. Businesses housing servers inside a colocation Data Center gain dependable uptime backed by trained facility personnel. Redundant cooling systems keep server temperatures stable across continuous operating cycles. Routine maintenance checks reduce equipment failure rates and extend hardware lifespans. Scalable rack space lets companies add servers without funding new construction projects. Is Colocation Different From Traditional Hosting? Yes, colocation is different from traditional hosting. Businesses own and maintain the physical servers housed inside a colocation facility. Traditional hosting providers supply the servers and retain ownership of the hardware. Management responsibilities differ across the two models. Colocation customers control software updates and security settings on owned servers. Traditional hosting providers manage software configurations on provider-owned hardware. Service models stay distinct since each option places different responsibilities on the client and the provider. Colocation suits companies needing direct hardware control, while traditional hosting suits companies seeking managed simplicity. Pricing structures reflect the ownership differences across the two service models. Why Do Businesses Use Colocation Services? Businesses use colocation services to access reliable power, cooling, and network resources without building private facilities. Colocation supports secure and scalable operations through monitored facilities and flexible rack space. Facilities provide specialized resources (redundant power feeds, climate control systems, trained security personnel). Reliability improves as multiple network carriers and backup generators reduce the risk of service interruptions. Companies avoid large capital spending tied to constructing and maintaining private server rooms. Scalable rack space lets businesses add equipment without funding new construction projects. Costs stay controlled through predictable monthly fees that replace unpredictable maintenance expenses. Shared facility resources lower spending compared with operating a private data center. Business continuity increases as redundant systems keep critical operations running during power outages. Disaster recovery plans benefit from geographically distributed colocation sites across separate regions. Trained personnel monitor equipment around the clock, reducing downtime caused by hardware failures. Companies gain dependable uptime without hiring large internal facility management teams. Predictable service agreements outline response times for technical support requests. What Resources Are Included in Colocation Services? Colocation services include core resources that support housed equipment inside a shared facility. Providers supply power, cooling, network connectivity, physical security, and rack space as standard components of the agreement. Each resource works together to keep servers operational, secure, and connected. The resources included in colocation services are listed below. Power Supply : The power supply delivers continuous electricity to housed servers through redundant feeds. Backup generators activate automatically during utility outages to prevent service interruptions. Cooling Systems : Cooling systems maintain stable temperatures inside server rooms through precision air handling units. Consistent climate control protects hardware from overheating and reduces component failure rates. Network Connectivity : Network connectivity enables data transfer through multiple carrier connections routed into the facility. Redundant paths maintain communication access during single connection failures. Physical Security : Physical security protects housed equipment through locked cages, biometric checkpoints, and continuous monitoring. Trained personnel control facility access around the clock. Rack Space : Rack space houses servers and hardware inside designated cabinets within the facility. Scalable rack configurations let companies add equipment without funding new construction projects. Can Companies Keep Their Own Servers in a Colocation Facility? Yes, companies can keep their own servers in a colocation facility. Ownership remains with the business throughout the agreement. Equipment stays under company control while staff configure and maintain installed hardware. Facility resources stay provider-managed (power, cooling, physical security systems). Flexibility is maintained since companies choose hardware specifications and software configurations independently. Reliability improves through redundant power feeds and monitored network connections. Businesses avoid funding private data centers while gaining dependable uptime. Scalable rack space lets companies add servers without long construction timelines. Trained personnel monitor housed equipment around the clock to limit unauthorized access. A colocation data center delivers core advantages that support business operations. Companies gain access to specialized resources without funding private facility construction. Each advantage strengthens reliability, security, and growth potential across housed equipment. The main advantages of a colocation data center are listed below. Improved Reliability : Redundant power feeds and backup generators keep operations running without interruption. Monitored network connections reduce downtime risk across continuous workloads. Trained personnel respond to equipment issues around the clock. Enhanced Security : Locked cages and biometric checkpoints protect housed equipment from unauthorized access. Continuous video monitoring tracks activity inside the facility around the clock. Layered security protocols safeguard stored data from physical threats. Scalability : Flexible rack space lets companies add servers as business needs grow. Scalable power and cooling resources support expanding equipment loads. Companies avoid funding new construction projects during periods of growth. Cost Efficiency : Predictable monthly fees replace large capital spending tied to private server rooms. Shared facility resources lower expenses compared with operating a private data center. Companies reduce maintenance costs tied to building power and cooling systems. Better Connectivity : Multiple carrier connections provide stable, low-latency network access. Redundant network paths maintain communication during single connection failures. Strong connectivity supports applications requiring continuous data transfer. How Can Colocation Improve Reliability and Uptime? Colocation improves reliability and uptime through redundant power systems and continuous monitoring. Critical equipment stays available during disruptions caused by utility outages or hardware failures. Backup generators activate automatically when primary power feeds fail. Redundant network carriers reduce downtime risks tied to single connection failures. Trained personnel monitor facility systems around the clock to catch issues early. Service availability improves as multiple layers of redundancy support continuous operations. Business operations remain stable since critical systems keep running during unexpected events. Scheduled maintenance checks prevent equipment failures from disrupting hosted workloads. Geographically distributed colocation sites support disaster recovery plans across separate regions. Service-level agreements define uptime targets and response times for technical support. Redundant cooling systems prevent overheating that damages sensitive hardware components. Companies gain dependable uptime without hiring large internal facility management teams. Does Colocation Reduce IT Costs? Yes, colocation reduces IT costs. Shared facility resources lower capital requirements tied to building private data centers. Facility expenses are split across multiple tenants, lowering spending on power and cooling systems. Capital investments tied to building systems decrease since companies rent space instead of constructing it. Cost efficiency improves as predictable monthly fees replace unpredictable maintenance expenses. Resource allocation becomes simpler when staff focuses on core business operations instead of facility upkeep. Companies avoid funding new construction projects tied to private server rooms. Colocation compares with cloud services through differences in ownership and resource delivery. Colocation provides rented space for company-owned hardware inside a shared facility. Cloud services provide virtualized resources hosted on shared platforms managed by external providers. The ownership model differs across the two services. Colocation customers control physical servers, while cloud customers access software-based resources. Colocation customers install, configure, and maintain owned equipment housed inside rented racks. Cloud customers access computing power through subscription plans without owning physical hardware. Physical equipment inside colocation facilities remains under direct company control throughout the agreement. Each model offers advantages, depending on operational priorities and technical requirements. Colocation suits companies needing direct hardware control and predictable performance levels. Cloud services suit companies seeking flexible scaling without managing physical equipment. Business needs determine selection since cost structures and control requirements vary across organizations. Companies needing strict compliance controls choose colocation for direct oversight. Pricing models differ across the two services. Colocation uses fixed monthly fees, while cloud services use usage-based billing. What Is the Difference Between Colocation and Cloud Computing? Colocation and cloud computing differ in hardware ownership and resource delivery. Colocation involves customer-owned hardware housed inside a provider facility. Cloud computing provides on-demand virtual resources hosted on shared provider platforms. Hardware ownership differs since colocation customers control physical servers directly. Resource delivery differs since cloud computing delivers computing power through subscription-based access. Each model supports IT operations through distinct technical and financial structures. Colocation suits companies needing direct equipment control and predictable performance. Cloud computing suits companies seeking flexible scaling without physical hardware management. Distinct approaches shape how companies plan capacity, budgets, and maintenance responsibilities. Colocation customers pay predictable monthly fees tied to rented rack space. Cloud computing customers pay usage-based fees tied to consumed processing power. Service-level agreements define performance expectations across the two service models. Companies select the approach that matches budget priorities and technical needs. Can Colocation and Cloud Be Used Together? Yes, colocation and cloud can be used together. Organizations combine rented rack space with cloud platforms to support varied workloads. Physical and cloud resources coexist inside combined deployments. Colocation houses core hardware while cloud platforms handle additional capacity. Stored equipment remains under direct company control while cloud services manage variable demand. Flexibility increases as companies shift workloads across platforms based on performance needs. Companies adjust resource allocation quickly without long procurement cycles. Workloads improve when sensitive data stays on owned hardware. Less critical tasks run on cloud platforms instead. Performance improves when workload placement matches application requirements. Scalability improves since cloud resources expand instantly without adding physical equipment. What Types of Colocation Services Are Available? Colocation services come in core formats that match different business needs. Providers offer options ranging from shared rack space to fully dedicated suites. Each format balances cost, control, and physical separation differently. The types of colocation services that are available are listed below. Rack Colocation : Rack colocation uses shared rack space inside a multi-tenant facility. Multiple businesses house equipment within the same rack structure. Shared power and cooling resources support each housed server. Cabinet Colocation : Cabinet colocation provides dedicated cabinets for housed equipment. Locked enclosures separate equipment from neighboring tenants inside the facility. Dedicated cabinets offer added security compared with shared rack space. Cage Colocation : Cage colocation offers enclosed areas built from floor-to-ceiling wire mesh. Enclosed cages separate equipment, restricting access to authorized personnel. Companies needing strict physical separation choose cage colocation for added control. Private Suites : Private suites provide dedicated rooms built within the larger facility. Walled rooms separate equipment fully from other tenants. Private suites suit companies needing maximum control over physical access. Managed Colocation : Managed colocation includes additional support services beyond basic rack space. Provider staff handles equipment monitoring, patching, and routine maintenance tasks. Managed services suit companies lacking dedicated internal IT personnel. How Do Managed Colocation Services Support Businesses? Managed colocation services support businesses through operational support for hosted equipment. Providers assist with routine maintenance and continuous monitoring of housed servers. Technical support stays available through dedicated facility staff and service-level agreements. Facility management stays simplified since providers handle power, cooling, and security systems. Internal workloads decrease as provider staff handles routine equipment checks. Operational efficiency improves through proactive monitoring of hosted systems. Monitoring catches issues before failures disrupt operations. Companies redirect internal staff toward core business priorities instead of facility upkeep. Managed services suit companies lacking dedicated technical personnel for equipment oversight. Scheduled patching and firmware updates keep hosted systems secure and current. Trained personnel respond to equipment alerts around the clock, reducing downtime risk. Predictable support contracts replace unpredictable in-house staffing and training expenses. Businesses gain dependable performance without building large internal technical teams. Are Managed Colocation Services Suitable for Small Companies? Support services include monitoring, maintenance, and routine equipment checks. Internal resource needs decrease since provider teams handle daily technical tasks. Scalability improves as small companies add equipment without hiring additional staff. Operational complexity decreases when providers manage power, cooling, and security systems. Small companies gain dependable performance without building large internal technical teams. Predictable support contracts replace unpredictable in-house staffing and training expenses. Trained personnel monitor housed equipment around the clock, reducing downtime risk. Small companies avoid funding large data center construction projects. How Do You Choose a Colocation Provider? To choose a colocation provider, follow the six steps. First, companies assess proximity to corporate offices and major network exchange points. Closer facilities reduce latency for on-site maintenance visits and equipment transport. Second, businesses review available bandwidth options and carrier diversity within the facility. Multiple carriers reduce connectivity risk tied to single network providers. Third, companies examine power redundancy and backup generator capacity across the site. Redundant power feeds protect critical equipment during utility outages. Fourth, businesses verify physical security measures (biometric access, video monitoring, staffed checkpoints). Layered security protocols protect housed equipment from unauthorized access. Fifth, companies compare pricing structures and contract terms across competing providers. Transparent pricing avoids unexpected fees tied to bandwidth overages or equipment changes. Lastly, businesses confirm service-level agreements that define uptime guarantees and support response times. Clear agreements set expectations for downtime compensation and maintenance response windows. Which Features Should You Look for in a Colocation Data Center? Selecting a colocation data center requires evaluating the infrastructure and services that support long-term reliability and business continuity. Strong operational capabilities help organizations reduce risks related to downtime, security breaches, and performance disruptions. Advanced Cooling : Advanced cooling systems protect equipment from overheating inside dense server environments. Precision air handling units maintain stable temperatures across racks. Consistent climate control extends hardware lifespan and reduces failure rates. Strong Connectivity : Strong connectivity improves network performance through multiple carrier connections. Redundant network paths reduce latency and prevent single points of failure. Reliable connectivity supports data-intensive applications and real-time operations. Physical Security : Physical security restricts unauthorized access through locked cages and biometric checkpoints. Continuous video monitoring tracks activity inside the facility. Layered security protocols protect housed equipment from theft or tampering. Technical Support : Technical support assists operations through on-site staff and remote monitoring services. Support teams respond to equipment alerts and routine maintenance needs. Available support reduces internal staffing demands for housed equipment. Is Security an Important Factor When Selecting a Provider? Yes, security is an important factor when selecting a provider. Security measures protect housed equipment and sensitive information from unauthorized access. Physical controls remain necessary inside facilities housing critical business data. Locked cages, biometric checkpoints, and monitored entry points limit access to authorized personnel. Monitoring systems hold value through continuous surveillance. Surveillance detects suspicious activity before incidents escalate. Risk decreases when layered security protocols cover physical and network access points. Compliance requirements gain support through documented security policies and audit trails. Providers offering certified security standards help companies meet industry regulations. Strong security practices protect stored data from breaches, theft, and unauthorized tampering. How Are Colocation Data Centers Used in Real World Applications? Colocation data centers support real-world applications across multiple industries requiring dependable operations. Business applications rely on reliable power, cooling, and network systems housed inside shared facilities. Industries use colocation facilities for critical operations tied to financial transactions, healthcare records, and manufacturing data. Systems remain available through redundant power feeds and monitored network connections. Data stays securely managed behind locked cages, biometric checkpoints, and continuous surveillance. Retail platforms depend on colocation facilities to process transactions during peak shopping periods. Streaming services use colocation resources to deliver content with minimal latency. Business continuity improves when redundant systems keep critical applications running during outages. Financial institutions maintain transaction processing through backup power and network redundancy. Healthcare organizations protect patient records behind layered physical and network security controls. Operational efficiency increases as colocation facilities handle routine maintenance and monitoring tasks. Manufacturing companies access production data continuously through stable network connections. Reduced downtime supports consistent service delivery across customer-facing platforms. events.before: Resources Data Centers Data Center Architecture: Design and Topology Data Center Architecture: Design and Topology Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 18 min read Published August 13, 2026 Updated October 30, 2026 Data Center Architecture refers to the structured design and organization of hardware, software, and infrastructure systems that support computing operations within a facility. Data Center Architecture establishes the framework for scalable, reliable, and secure infrastructure, setting standards for capacity planning, redundancy, and risk management. The design process addresses physical layout, equipment placement, and system redundancy to prevent downtime and data loss. Reliability depends on redundant power sources, cooling systems, and network pathways that maintain continuous operations during equipment failures or scheduled maintenance. Security measures, including access controls and monitoring systems, protect physical assets and sensitive data from unauthorized access or breaches. Core components of the architecture include network topology, power distribution, cooling infrastructure, and physical facility design, each contributing to system performance. Topology determines how servers, switches, and storage devices connect, influencing data flow efficiency and fault tolerance across the network. Power systems (uninterruptible power supplies and backup generators) sustain operations during outages and support peak workload demands. Physical design elements (server racks, floor layout, and containment strategies) optimize space utilization and airflow management. Modern architecture accommodates enterprise applications and cloud workloads by enabling flexible scaling, distributed computing, and virtualization across multiple locations. What Is Data Center Architecture? Data center architecture is a structured design of physical infrastructure, network topology, and system components that support computing operations within a facility. Architecture combines hardware placement, cabling standards, and equipment configuration into a unified framework that determines capacity, performance, and reliability across the environment. Physical architecture covers tangible elements (server racks, cooling units, power distribution systems), while logical architecture governs data flow, network segmentation, and virtualization layers. The two layers operate together, forming a foundation that supports growth without compromising uptime or security standards across facilities. Physical and logical architecture remain interdependent, since equipment placement directly influences how logical systems perform under load. Cabling paths, rack configurations, and cooling zones establish the physical boundaries within which logical networks route traffic and manage workloads. A high-level architecture diagram illustrates the relationship, showing how racks, switches, and storage arrays map to network segments and virtual environments. Facility planners reference related topics (power distribution, cooling design, network topology) when documenting What is Data Center architecture, since the answer depends on physical layout as much as logical configuration across the entire system. What Are the Core Components of Data Center Architecture? Data center architecture relies on six interdependent components that work together to deliver consistent performance and uptime. Each element serves a distinct function, yet failure in one area affects the reliability of the entire system. The core components of data center architecture are listed below. Compute : Servers process application workloads and execute the calculations that power enterprise systems. Compute resources scale through virtualization, allowing multiple workloads to run on shared hardware. Storage : Storage systems retain data across drives, arrays, and distributed file systems for retrieval and backup. Redundant storage configurations protect against data loss during hardware failures. Networking : Switches, routers, and cabling connect compute and storage resources, enabling data transfer within and beyond the facility. Network design determines latency, bandwidth, and fault tolerance across connected systems. Power : Uninterruptible power supplies and backup generators maintain continuous electricity during outages. Power distribution units regulate voltage and prevent equipment damage from fluctuations. Cooling : Cooling systems regulate temperature and humidity, preventing equipment overheating during peak operational loads. Airflow management (hot aisle and cold aisle containment) improves cooling efficiency. Security : Access controls, surveillance systems, and firewalls protect physical and digital assets from unauthorized entry. Security protocols form part of the broader Components of Data Center design, since protection measures integrate directly with facility layout and network architecture. How Has Data Center Architecture Evolved? Data center architecture has evolved through four distinct stages, moving from traditional standalone systems toward flexible, distributed models. Traditional architecture relied on dedicated physical servers assigned to specific applications, resulting in underutilized hardware and limited scalability during demand spikes. Virtualized architecture introduced software layers that partitioned physical servers into multiple virtual machines, improving resource utilization and reducing hardware costs across facilities. Hyperconverged architecture consolidated compute, storage, and networking into unified software-defined systems, simplifying management and enabling faster deployment through standardized building blocks. Cloud-based architecture extended the principles further, distributing workloads across remote facilities and allowing organizations to scale capacity without owning physical infrastructure. Technological advancements (software-defined networking, automated orchestration, edge computing) accelerated the shift toward flexible, distributed models over the past two decades. Each stage addressed limitations of the previous model, prioritizing efficiency, redundancy, and cost reduction. Modern facilities combine elements from multiple stages, blending on-premises hyperconverged systems with cloud-based resources to balance control and scalability across enterprise workloads. What Are the Main Types of Data Center Architecture? Data center architecture comes in distinct models, each suited to different operational needs and budget constraints. Selection depends on workload requirements, scalability targets, and available capital for infrastructure investment. Organizations weigh factors (redundancy needs, growth projections, management overhead) before committing to a specific model. The main types of data center architectures are shown in the table below. Architecture Type Description Advantages Limitations Best Use Case Architecture Type Traditional Description Dedicated physical servers support applications within a single facility. Advantages Offers direct hardware control and predictable performance. Limitations Requires high capital investment and underutilizes resources. Best Use Case Suited for legacy systems with fixed workloads. Architecture Type Virtualized Description Software layers partition physical servers into multiple virtual machines. Advantages Improves hardware utilization and lowers operating costs. Limitations Depends on hypervisor performance and licensing expenses. Best Use Case Fits mid-size enterprises consolidating server fleets. Architecture Type Hyperconverged Description Compute, storage, and networking merge into unified software-defined systems. Advantages Simplifies management and speeds deployment timelines. Limitations Limits customization compared to component-based systems. Best Use Case Works well for organizations seeking rapid scaling. Architecture Type Cloud-Based Description One of the common Types of Data Center models, workloads are distributed across remote facilities managed by third-party providers. Advantages Delivers elastic scaling without owning physical hardware. Limitations Raises concerns around data control and recurring costs. Best Use Case Serves businesses with variable or seasonal demand. What Is Enterprise Data Center Architecture? Enterprise data center architecture is the design framework organizations use to support large-scale computing operations across business units and departments. Design objectives center on aligning infrastructure investment with operational demands, ensuring systems handle current workloads while accommodating future growth. Scalability requirements dictate that the architecture support expansion by adding compute, storage, or network capacity without disrupting existing operations. Resilience standards mandate redundant systems across power, cooling, and network pathways to minimize downtime during equipment failures or maintenance windows. Governance requirements establish policies for access control, compliance reporting, and change management across the facility. A reference architecture example includes tiered network segments, redundant power feeds, and virtualized compute pools distributed across multiple zones. Organizations structure Enterprise Data Center architecture around the principles to balance performance, cost control, and regulatory compliance across departments and business units. What Is Multi Data Center Architecture? Multi data center architecture is the design approach connecting two or more geographically separated facilities into a coordinated infrastructure system. Distributed facilities operate as interconnected nodes, sharing workloads and replicating data across locations to reduce dependency on any single site. Geographic separation protects operations against regional outages (natural disasters, power grid failures, network disruptions) that otherwise halt business functions entirely. Disaster recovery capabilities improve under the model, since backup sites activate automatically when a primary facility experiences failure. High availability relies on synchronized data replication and load balancing across sites, maintaining consistent application performance regardless of location. Workload distribution allows organizations to route traffic toward the facility with the lowest latency or the highest capacity at any given time. A topology diagram illustrating multiple sites shows primary and secondary facilities connected through dedicated network links, with data flowing bidirectionally to maintain synchronization across the distributed system. What Is Modern Data Center Network Architecture? Modern data center network architecture is the design approach using flat, high-bandwidth topologies and software-driven controls to support dynamic workloads. Spine-leaf networking replaces traditional hierarchical models by connecting each leaf switch directly to each spine switch, reducing latency and eliminating bottlenecks common in older designs. Software-defined networking (SDN) separates the network control plane from physical hardware, allowing administrators to manage traffic flow through centralized software rather than manual device configuration. Virtualization extends the flexibility further, enabling multiple logical networks to operate across shared physical infrastructure without interference. Automation tools reduce manual configuration tasks, deploying network changes across hundreds of devices within minutes rather than hours. Traditional network designs relied on three-tier hierarchies (core, aggregation, access layers) that introduced multiple hops and increased latency between servers. Modern architectures eliminate the inefficiencies through flatter topologies and programmable controls, supporting the low-latency demands of cloud computing and high-density virtualized environments. A modern network topology diagram illustrates spine and leaf switches interconnected in a mesh pattern, contrasting sharply with the layered structure of legacy network designs. What Is Data Center Network Architecture? Data center network architecture is the design framework governing how switches, routers, and cabling connect compute and storage resources within a facility. Network design directly influences infrastructure performance, determining data transfer speeds, latency, and fault tolerance across connected systems. Poorly designed networks create bottlenecks that slow application response times and limit the facility's ability to handle peak workloads. Well-structured architecture distributes traffic efficiently across multiple pathways, preventing single points of failure from disrupting operations. Network architecture supports compute and storage by providing the pathways through which data moves between servers, storage arrays, and end users. Compute resources depend on low-latency connections to access shared storage systems, while storage arrays rely on sufficient bandwidth to handle simultaneous read and write requests from multiple servers. An overview network diagram illustrates core switches, aggregation layers, and access points connecting racks of servers to centralized storage systems. Redundant pathways within the diagram show how traffic reroutes automatically during equipment failures, maintaining continuous operations across compute and storage layers without manual intervention. What Network Layers Make Up a Data Center Architecture? Data center architecture organizes network traffic through distinct layers, each handling a specific function within the system. Traffic flows upward from servers through the layers before reaching external networks, or follows equivalent paths within spine-leaf designs. The network layers that make up a data center architecture are listed below. Core layer : The core layer connects aggregation switches and routes traffic between different sections of the facility. High-speed links within the layer minimize latency during large-scale data transfers. Aggregation layer : The aggregation layer consolidates traffic from multiple access switches before forwarding it to the core. Redundant connections at the layer prevent single points of failure during equipment outages. Access layer : The access layer connects directly to servers and storage devices within separate racks. Switches at this level handle the highest volume of localized traffic within the facility. Edge layer : The edge layer manages traffic entering and exiting the facility toward external networks or remote users. Security appliances and load balancers commonly operate at the boundary point. Spine-leaf equivalent : Spine switches connect directly to each leaf switch, replacing the traditional three-tier hierarchy with a flatter structure. Leaf switches connect to servers, forwarding traffic through spine switches for consistent, low-latency paths across the network. How Do Network Topology Designs Improve Performance? Network topology designs improve performance by structuring connections to minimize latency, increase throughput, and eliminate single points of failure. Selection among available topologies depends on facility size, workload demands, and redundancy requirements across the infrastructure. Latency decreases when data travels through fewer hops between source and destination points. Scalability, redundancy, and throughput each factor into which topology suits a given deployment. Network topology designs that improve performance are shown in the table below. Topology Benefits Limitations Common Deployment Topology Spine-Leaf Benefits Delivers consistent low latency through direct leaf-to-spine connections. Limitations Requires more cabling and switch ports than hierarchical designs. Common Deployment Fits large-scale cloud and virtualized environments. Topology Three-Tier Benefits Provides straightforward hierarchical management and troubleshooting. Limitations Introduces higher latency through multiple hops between layers. Common Deployment Suits smaller facilities with predictable traffic patterns. Topology Mesh Benefits Offers high redundancy through multiple interconnected paths. Limitations Increases complexity and cost as node count grows. Common Deployment Applies to facilities requiring maximum fault tolerance. Topology Ring Benefits Simplifies cabling through sequential device connections. Limitations Limits throughput and creates vulnerability at single breaks. Common Deployment Serves smaller or legacy network segments. How Is Data Center Power Architecture Designed? Data center power architecture is designed to deliver electricity from utility sources to IT equipment through a sequence of transformers, switchgear, and distribution units. Utility power enters the facility at high voltage before stepping down through transformers to levels usable by internal systems. Switchgear routes electricity toward uninterruptible power supplies, which condition the current and provide immediate backup during momentary outages. Power distribution units then deliver electricity to individual racks, regulating voltage and preventing fluctuations from damaging sensitive equipment. Redundancy concepts guide design decisions at each stage, ensuring backup systems activate automatically when primary power sources fail. Backup generators supply extended power during prolonged outages, starting within seconds of a utility failure. Dual power feeds from separate utility substations protect against single points of failure at the source level. A simplified power flow diagram illustrates the sequence, showing electricity moving from utility lines through transformers, switchgear, and UPS systems before reaching distribution units and, finally, individual server racks. What Are the Essential Components of Data Center Power Architecture? Data center power architecture depends on components working together to deliver reliable, uninterrupted electricity to IT equipment. Each element serves a distinct function within the power chain, from initial distribution through backup activation. The essential components of data center power architecture are listed below. Switchgear : Switchgear controls and routes electrical current from utility sources toward downstream systems within the facility. Circuit breakers within switchgear protect equipment by interrupting current during faults or overloads. Uninterruptible power supply : The uninterruptible power supply conditions incoming electricity and provides instant backup during momentary outages or voltage fluctuations. Battery systems within the UPS bridge the gap until generators activate. Generators : Generators supply extended backup power during prolonged utility outages, activating within seconds of a failure. Diesel or natural gas fuel sources sustain generator operation for hours or days depending on capacity. Power distribution units : Power distribution units deliver regulated electricity from upstream systems directly to server racks and equipment. Redundancy improves power reliability by ensuring backup systems compensate automatically when primary components fail, preventing service interruptions. N configuration portrays the baseline capacity required to support a facility's power load without any backup components beyond standard operation. N+1 configuration adds one additional component beyond baseline capacity, allowing a single failure to occur without affecting operations. 2N configuration duplicates the entire power system, providing two fully independent paths so that either path alone supports the complete facility load. Planners calculate projected compute, storage, and power needs based on current workloads and anticipated growth. Requirements gathered during the phase influence facility size and equipment specifications throughout later stages. Select a site location . Site selection accounts for factors (proximity to power grids, natural disaster risk, network connectivity) that affect long-term operational stability. Climate conditions influence cooling system design and energy efficiency. Design the physical layout . Floor plans establish rack placement, aisle configuration, and equipment zones to optimize space and airflow.
